title: Quick start
description: Go from an empty project to a background job that a worker picks up and runs.
headings: Check it with the sample host
body: This page builds one small console app that is both a producer and a worker. It dispatches a job, and its own worker runs it. The same job and handler work unchanged when you later split them into a web app and a separate worker service. You need the .NET 10 SDK and one store. Docker is the quickest way to get PostgreSQL or Redis; SQLite needs nothing. Runwick refuses a Redis server without these durability settings. Create Jobs.cs . A job is a record that implements IQueueJob and has a [JobName] . The name is what gets stored, so you can rename or move the C type later without breaking jobs already in the store. The handler is created from dependency injection, in a fresh scope for each run, so constructor injection works as usual. IJobContext tells it which job and which execution it is on. Workers never create the schema themselves. Run the migration once, before the app starts. In a real deployment this is a separate step with its own credentials; here it runs at the top of Program.cs to keep things short. Delete the template's Worker.cs and replace Program.cs with: You can run the same migration from the command line instead: runwick migrate --provider postgres --connection-env MY CONN . See Installation. Continue Program.cs below the migration. Only the Use... line depends on the store. - Application("quickstart") names your app inside the store, so several apps can share one database. - AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining registers every [JobName] type in that assembly. - AddWorker makes this process a worker. Pool main reads queue default and runs at most 4 jobs at once. Jobs with no [Queue] go to default . Leave out AddWorker in an app that only dispatches. Add this after StartAsync : Run it: You should see the Dispatched job line, then the handler's log line a moment later. Press Ctrl + C to stop. The worker stops taking new jobs and gives running ones time to finish. In a web app, inject IJobDispatcher into an endpoint or a service instead of resolving it by hand: What just happened DispatchAsync returned only after the store confirmed the job was written. The worker found the job, took a lease on it, ran your handler in its own dependency-injection scope, and recorded the result as succeeded . If the handler had thrown, the job would have waited a few seconds and run again. By default a job runs at most 3 times, so 2 automatic retries, before it ends up failed . A network failure can leave DispatchAsync unable to tell whether the write happened. The job may or may not exist. Dispatching and Delivery guarantees explain how to handle it safely. Check it with the sample host The repository ships a sample host for PostgreSQL that migrates, dispatches a batch of jobs, runs them on an in-process worker, and prints how many succeeded: It prints 10 succeeded and exits with code 0 when every job ran. Add the dashboard (optional) The dashboard runs inside an ASP.NET Core app and needs your own sign-in, such as cookie authentication registered with AddAuthentication().AddCookie() and app.UseAuthentication() . There is no anonymous mode. This example gives every signed-in user the Operator role; map roles from your own claims in a real app. Sign in, open /runwick , and you can see the job, its attempts and its status history. Dashboard covers permissions and setup in full. Next steps Queues, priorities, execution limits and the fluent alternative to attributes. Change the retry budget and delay, and set an execution timeout. Pools, concurrency, shutdown and running workers in a separate process. Why handlers must be safe to repeat, and how to make them so.

title: Retention
description: How Runwick deletes old payloads, finished jobs, audit rows and history, and how to tune the cleanup.
body: Without cleanup, payloads, errors, finished jobs, audit rows and history would grow forever. Every worker process runs a background cleanup loop that removes old records in small, resumable batches. It never removes a record that something still depends on, and it never touches a job that is waiting, running or retrying. What gets deleted, and when There is one retention policy per application. Each kind of record has its own age limit: Policy value Default What it removes --- --- --- Completed detail 7 days Payload and error text of jobs that succeeded or were cancelled Failed detail 30 days Payload and error text of failed jobs Job history 90 days The rest of a finished job (its row, generations, attempts) and its events Audit 90 days Management audit rows Scaling events 7 days Automatic concurrency history Schedule occurrences 30 days Which schedule fires created which jobs Worker presence 24 hours after expiry Heartbeat rows of workers that went away Jobs go in two steps. First the detail expires: payload and error text are deleted, but the job's identity, state and history stay, and the job is marked "detail expired". Revealing its payload then answers 410 detail expired . Later, once job history expires, the whole job goes. After that a lookup by its ID answers 404 , and nothing tells it apart from an ID that never existed. Some records follow fixed rules that no policy can shorten: command receipts until their replay window ends, uniqueness keys until their window ends, rate-limit grants until they leave the rate window, outbox mappings until 24 hours past their horizon. Concurrency scopes, queue controls and schedules are never deleted. Changing the policy The policy is edited through the management API or the dashboard's Retention page, with the Retention.Manage permission. Every edit is checked against the current revision and audited. There is no CLI command for it. Post that body to {prefix}/v1/retention/policy with the antiforgery header. Revision 0 means the defaults are still in force. Rules: - Every value is whole hours, from 1 to 87,600 (ten years). - Audit is kept at least 7 days. - Job history must be at least as long as both detail values. - null means keep forever, except worker presence, which is required. A value you leave out of the body is read as null , which means keep forever . Read the current policy first and send all seven values back. Tuning the cleanup loop The loop runs in every process that calls AddWorker . Producer-only processes, schedulers and the standalone management host do not run it. Several workers cooperate through a progress row per record class, so only one batch of a class runs at a time and cleanup resumes where it stopped after a crash. RetentionOptions Default Allowed --- --- --- Enabled true BatchRows 100 1 to 1,000 rows per batch BatchDetailBytes 1 MiB 64 KiB to 16 MiB of payload and error text per batch BatchTarget 500 ms 50 ms to 2 s of database time a batch aims at BatchPause 1 s 0 to 60 s between batches of one class IdlePoll 60 s 1 s to 1 h after a pass that found nothing A failed batch backs off from 5 seconds, doubling up to 5 minutes. Values outside the bounds stop the app at startup. Cleanup is bounded work Each process runs one batch at a time. It skips rows that are locked, so it never waits on live work, and it pauses while the worker is draining or under pressure. At the defaults that is roughly 100 rows a second for one busy class in one process. A store that finishes more than about 5 million jobs a day needs bigger batches, shorter pauses or more worker processes. Cleanup does not promise to keep up with any load. It tells you when it falls behind: - the dashboard's Retention page shows each class's progress and marks a class "behind" when no pass caught up in the last 24 hours; - the runwick.retention.caught up.age gauge and the RunwickRetentionFailing alert (see Observability); - log events 1501 (batch failed) and 1503 (behind). Cleanup itself writes one summary audit row per class per day, not one row per deleted record. Those rows do not list which rows were deleted. Cleanup never changes a health check. Backups and copies Deleting a row does not erase it from backups, replicas, exports or log pipelines. If you have a legal reason to remove data, you also need a retention plan for those copies. Runwick has no "delete this job now" request and no legal hold. Restoring a backup brings old rows back; the cleanup loop removes them again on its next passes. See Upgrades for what else a restore changes.

title: Upgrades and restores
description: How to upgrade Runwick safely, why there is no rolling upgrade, and what a restore from backup does and does not bring back.
body: Read this before your first upgrade. One rule shapes everything else: A Runwick release works with exactly one store revision. Once the new schema is in place, the previous release cannot run at all: it cannot create work and it cannot finish work. There are no down migrations. The only way back is the backup you took before migrating. So an upgrade is a short stop of new work: drain, stop the old processes, migrate, reopen, start the new ones . Plan for that, not for a rolling deploy. Before you start - Use the CLI from the new release for migrate , and the currently deployed CLI for the store commands before migrating. Check with runwick version . - Have the migration-role credentials. The app's runtime role cannot run these commands. - Know every process that uses the store: workers, producers, schedulers, dashboards, CLI hosts. You must be able to stop each one. Runwick cannot stop them for you, and cannot prove that they stopped. The examples use PostgreSQL. Use --provider sqlite with a database file, or --provider redis with a Redis configuration string, the same way. RUNWICK STORE is the name of an environment variable holding the migration-role connection string. Upgrade, step by step PostgreSQL: pg dump -Fc mydb before-upgrade.dump . SQLite: stop every process on the file and copy it (with its -wal and -shm files), or run sqlite3 runwick.db ".backup before-upgrade.db" . Redis: copy the AOF or RDB files the way you normally do. store status shows the store revision, the revision this CLI expects, each application's admission mode, and how many leases and worker heartbeats exist. Drain stops all new work (dispatch, claims, scheduled jobs, retries) and lets running work keep renewing and finish. Add --application NAME to drain one application. If you get migration lock timeout , a transaction that stages jobs has been open for over 5 seconds. Wait and try again. Run store status until it shows no owned leases, or decide to abandon what remains (an abandoned lease expires and the new version recovers it). Then stop the old workers, producers, schedulers and dashboards yourself. Do not read an expired lease or an expired heartbeat as "stopped". A paused or cut-off process looks exactly the same. It prints the store ID, the new revision and what it applied. Running it again applies nothing. Reopen before starting the new processes. A process that starts while its application is drained is refused at startup with AdmissionClosedException , because registering its queues counts as new work. Nothing was written; reopen and start it again. Start workers, then producers, then dashboards. Check with runwick doctor --connection-env RUNWICK STORE (the revision check passes when the CLI and the store agree) and store status . If migrate fails Code Meaning What to do --- --- --- migration connection lost The session holding the migration lock died Run again; it resumes where it stopped migration lock timeout , migration lock unavailable Another migrator, or a long transaction Wait, run again schema validation failed Something in the database differs from what this release expects Do not force it. The store stays at the last good revision and no release can run on it. Read the message, repair or restore, run again migration checksum mismatch A released migration was changed Stop. You are running a different build from the one that migrated this store migration unknown The store is newer than this CLI You are rolling back by accident. Use the matching CLI, or restore If it goes wrong - Before migrate finished: nothing changed shape. Reopen with --mode open and keep running the old release. - After migrate: the old release cannot run. Restore the backup from step 1 and run the old release with the old CLI. Work done after the backup is lost. - An old process is still running: its next call is refused and nothing is written. Stop it anyway. Capabilities cannot be undone scheduler and rate admission are turned on with runwick store activate-capability . That is a second one-way door, separate from migrations: - A capability is never lowered. There is no command to turn it off. - A release that does not know the capability can no longer create work for that application. It can still renew and finish jobs it already holds. - Each activation writes an audit row and an event. Activate only after every process on the store runs a release that supports it. Schedules after an upgrade - While an application is drained, the scheduler creates no jobs and its position does not move. After reopening, each schedule's misfire policy decides what happens to the fires it missed: skipped, run once, or caught up. - If a new release brings a new schedule evaluator or new time-zone data, roll the release out to every scheduler host first, and only then change schedule definitions to use it. A host that does not know the new version skips that schedule and says so in its logs. Restoring from a backup A restore is a step back in time, and Runwick cannot tell that it happened. After a restore: - jobs and results written after the backup are gone; - a dispatch your callers saw succeed may now be unknown, and resending it creates the job again unless its idempotency key survived; - schedules move back and their fires run again or are skipped, following each schedule's misfire policy; - fencing tokens and rate-limit windows can hand out values they already handed out; - outbox messages delivered after the backup may be delivered again. Runwick does not undo emails sent or payments taken in the lost window. You reconcile those. Replace, or copy? Situation Identity --- --- Replace a broken store. The original is gone and will never run again Keep the store ID Copy that runs beside the original (staging, inspection, disaster-recovery rehearsal) Give it a new ID before anything connects When unsure, give it a new ID. A new ID is harmless. A duplicate ID lets commands meant for one store land in the other. Workers, producers, schedulers, dashboards, CLI hosts. If the old store is still reachable, put it in maintenance so a straggler is refused: store admission --mode drain , then --mode maintenance . Maintenance can only be reached from drain. PostgreSQL: createdb restored && pg restore -d restored --no-owner before-upgrade.dump . SQLite: copy the file back. Redis: restore the AOF the way you normally do. A backup from an older schema needs the older release and CLI if you want to stay on that release. reidentify refuses unless every application is in maintenance and the store records no live leases or heartbeats. Right after a restore it may refuse because the backup carried heartbeats of processes that were running; wait until they expire. After it succeeds, anything bound to the old ID is refused with store identity mismatch and nothing is written. store admission --mode open , then start the processes. Go through effects outside the database, lost acknowledgements, schedules, fences and outbox deliveries, as listed above. Decide per job type whether to run again or suppress. What Runwick does not promise - No mixed-version operation, no rolling upgrade across schema revisions, no zero-downtime migration. Drain pauses new work, not running work. - No downgrade. Rolling back means restoring, and restoring loses what came after the backup. - No proof that an old process has stopped, from leases, heartbeats or time. - No automatic detection of a copy. You must re-identify it yourself. - Admission and identity changes write no audit row. Capability activations do.

title: Deployment
description: Process shapes, containers, the migration step, shutdown timeouts, capabilities and a checklist for going live.
body: Runwick has no server of its own. It runs inside your processes, and the store (PostgreSQL, SQLite or Redis) is the only shared part. What a process does is decided by its configuration, not by which program it is. Roles Role Turned on by --- --- Producer Always: any process with AddRunwick can dispatch Worker AddWorker(...) Scheduler AddScheduler() Management host MapRunwickManagement(...) and/or MapRunwickDashboard(...) A process can have any combination. Common shapes One web app dispatches, runs workers, runs the scheduler and serves the dashboard. Simplest to run, and fine for many apps. The trade-off: a slow job and a web request compete for the same CPU, and every deploy restarts both. The web app only dispatches (no AddWorker ). A separate worker service, built with Host.CreateApplicationBuilder , runs the handlers. The two can share a contracts project with Runwick.Contracts , so the web app needs no handler code. You can scale and deploy the two separately. Several identical instances, each dispatching and working. Every replica claims from the same store; leases make sure one job has one owner at a time. Keep in mind: concurrency limits declared on jobs and queues hold across replicas, because they are kept in the store. But rate limits on the management API, the producer's local limits and the automatic concurrency controller work per process . Ten replicas allow ten times the management API rate. SQLite supports all of these only when every process is on the same machine. See Choosing a store. Migrations are a separate step Runwick does not migrate the store when your app starts. Run migrations as a deploy step, with credentials that may create schemas: or from code, for example in a one-off job: The running app can then use a role that only reads and writes data. migrate is safe to run again: a second run applies nothing. A binary works with exactly one store revision. A process that meets a store at another revision refuses to run. So on an upgrade the migration step is part of a short stop of new work, not something you can roll out replica by replica. Upgrades has the procedure. Containers and shutdown The worker needs up to 25 seconds to stop cleanly (drain, then cancel, then write results). Give it room at every layer: Layer Default Set it to --- --- --- Runwick ShutdownBudget 25 s Leave it, or change the slices in Workers .NET HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout 30 s Above Runwick's budget Container grace period (Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds ) 30 s Above the host's timeout If a process is killed early, no data is lost, but its running jobs wait for their leases to expire (60 seconds by default) before another worker takes them. Handlers should honour their CancellationToken so the cancel step finishes in time. Map health checks: liveness on the live tag, readiness on ready . A draining worker is not ready but still alive, so the orchestrator stops routing to it without restarting it. Capabilities Schedules and rate limits need a capability turned on once per application, by an operator: Feature Capability Error without it --- --- --- AddScheduler , AddSchedule scheduler Startup fails with scheduler not active RollingWindow(...) rate limits rate admission Dispatching a rate-limited job is refused with rate admission not active ; nothing is written The order is: start the application once so it registers itself, activate, restart. Once raised, a capability stays. A binary that does not know it can no longer create work for that application. Activate only when every process that uses the store runs a release that supports it. Checklist PostgreSQL 16 to 18 connected directly to the primary; SQLite on a local disk; Redis 8.2 or newer, one primary, with appendfsync always and noeviction . Runwick refuses unsafe settings at startup. runwick migrate with the migration role, before the app starts. Use the CLI from the same release. scheduler and rate admission , once per application, after its first start. Runwick 25 s, host above that, container grace period above the host. AddHealthChecks().AddRunwick() , with live and ready endpoints wired to your orchestrator. Real sign-in, a grant mapping you have reviewed, HTTPS. Share the Data Protection key ring across replicas. Traces and metrics through OpenTelemetry. Turn on CollectApplicationMetrics in one process, import the Grafana dashboard and the alert rules, and tune the thresholds. Back up the store like any database you depend on, and read Upgrades before the first upgrade, not during it.

title: AI agents
description: Give coding agents Runwick's docs as plain text, let them drive the runwick CLI in --agent mode, and the conventions worth putting in AGENTS.md.
headings: Point the agent at the docs
Rules that differ in agent mode
Let the agent check its own work
body: Coding agents work well with Runwick when they know three things: where the docs are, which rules are easy to get wrong (at-least-once, stable job names, no auto-migration), and how to inspect and change a running system safely. This page gives you all three. Point the agent at the docs The documentation is published as plain text for language models: URL Contents --- --- https://runwick.temtem.dev/llms.txt An index of every page with a one-line summary, in the llms.txt format. https://runwick.temtem.dev/llms-full.txt The whole documentation in one Markdown file. Agents that can fetch URLs can read these directly. For agents that cannot, download llms-full.txt into your repository (for example as docs/runwick.md ) and reference it from your agent instructions. Add an AGENTS.md section Most coding agents read a project instruction file: AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md , .github/copilot-instructions.md or .cursor/rules . Copy this section and adjust it to your app: The CLI in agent mode The runwick command line talks to a running management API (and, for migrate , store ... and doctor , to the database). Add --agent to any command and it prints exactly one JSON object per command on standard output, on one line, with no colour, no prompts and no pager: Field Meaning --- --- ok , result , error result is the same object --output json prints. error has a stable code , whether it is retryable , and a hint . commandId Set for every change, also on failure, so the agent can re-send the same command. revisions The revision of every target seen, ready for the next change. nextActions Suggested follow-up commands as full argv arrays. They are suggestions: the CLI does not know your permissions. Streaming commands ( jobs tail , events tail ) print one envelope per line (JSON Lines), with "stream": "item" on each item and a final "stream": "end" line. Learn the tool: runwick --agent describe This prints one envelope whose result lists every command, its arguments and options (with which ones are required in agent mode), its permission, a JSON Schema of its result, the envelope schema, every error code with its hint, and the exit codes. An agent can learn the CLI from it without reading these pages. Exit codes Code Meaning --- --- 0 ok 1 rejected (for example stale revision , not found ) 2 usage error 3 outcome unknown: re-send with the same --command-id 4 unavailable (for example connection failed , store unavailable ) 5 unauthenticated or forbidden Rules that differ in agent mode - No prompts. A missing secret fails at once with credential missing . Give it through the context's secret variable, RUNWICK SECRET , or --secret-stdin . - Expected revisions are required. In human mode, a change without --expected-revision reads the target first. In agent mode it is a usage error whose next action is the read to run. This keeps an agent from overwriting a change it never saw. - --agent and --output cannot be combined, and --verbose is ignored. Tips for agents operating Runwick - Read, then change. Run jobs get , queues list or schedules list first, and pass the revision from revisions to the change. On stale revision or stale generation , read again and decide again; do not just retry with the new number. - Re-send, do not repeat. On exit code 3 ( outcome unknown ), re-send the same command with the same --command-id . A new command ID is a new request. - Payloads are never printed by accident. Only jobs reveal-payload and jobs reveal-error show them, and each writes an audit row. Do not reveal payloads unless the task needs it. - Connection strings stay out of argv. migrate , store ... and doctor take --connection-env or --connection-stdin , never a connection string as an argument. - Store administration is a deliberate step. store admission , store activate-capability and store reidentify change the whole application and need the migration role. Activating a capability cannot be undone. Ask a human first. - Use --reason . Every change takes --reason , which is recorded in the audit trail. Say that an agent made the change and why. - Check the setup with runwick doctor . It checks the connection, credentials and settings and reports failed checks with check failed . Let the agent check its own work Ask the agent to finish with dotnet build and dotnet test , including an end-to-end test against a temporary SQLite file for any new job (see Testing). A test that calls the handler twice with the same job is a cheap way to catch handlers that are not safe to repeat.

title: Queues and priorities
description: Route jobs to queues, use the high, medium and low priority lanes, tune weights and aging, and pause a queue.
headings: Putting a job in a queue
body: A queue is a named stream of jobs, such as emails or reports . Workers subscribe to queues. Inside each queue there are three priority lanes : high , medium and low . A lane is one queue and priority pair. Every job has exactly one queue and one priority. The defaults are queue default and priority medium . Putting a job in a queue A single dispatch can override both: Registering queues A queue exists once something registers it. A job whose effective queue is emails registers emails . You can also declare a queue directly, which is also where you give it a concurrency cap: Dispatching to an unregistered queue fails with unknown queue . Queue names follow the name grammar: 1 to 128 characters of A-Z a-z 0-9 . - , case-sensitive. Subscribing workers A worker has one or more pools . Each pool subscribes to queues and has its own number of slots: Queues(...) gives each queue weight 1. Queue(name, weight) sets a weight from 1 to 1,000. When several queues in a pool have work, weights decide how often each gets the next free slot. With reports at 1 and pdf at 3, about three in four claims go to pdf . Subscriptions are explicit. Registering a handler never subscribes a pool to anything. A job in a queue no pool subscribes to simply waits. See Workers for pool sizing. Priority lanes Priority is not a sort order. Each pool picks a lane using weighted round robin , with default weights high 6, medium 3, low 1. When all three lanes in a queue have work, roughly 60% of claims come from high , 30% from medium and 10% from low . Low-priority work keeps moving; it just moves more slowly. You can change the weights per pool. Each must be from 1 to 1,000: Weights share out chances to claim a job. They do not reserve CPU, they do not interrupt a running job, and a long job holds its slot as long as it runs. Aging In the default mode a lower lane that has waited a long time gets an extra turn. After 8 claims from a queue, if the oldest eligible job in a lower lane has waited at least 60 seconds, the next claim goes to that lane. These two numbers are fixed. Aging changes the ratios on purpose so that low jobs do not wait forever behind a steady stream of high jobs. It is not a start-time guarantee, and it never changes a job's stored priority. Lane selection modes Mode Behaviour --- --- Weighted (default) Weighted round robin, with aging. StrictWithAging Always the highest lane that has work, with aging as the escape valve. Strict Always the highest lane that has work. No aging. In Strict mode a steady supply of high jobs means low jobs never run. Use it only when that is what you want. Between queues, the choice is always weighted, whatever the lane mode. Pausing a queue Pausing a queue stops workers from claiming new jobs from it. That is all it does: - Jobs already running keep running and finish normally. - Dispatching into a paused queue still works. Jobs pile up as pending . - Nothing is cancelled or released. Resume the queue and workers pick the backlog up again. Every change carries the queue revision you last saw. If someone else changed the queue in between, you get a conflict instead of a surprise. Pauses and resumes are written to the audit trail. The dashboard has the same buttons; see Dashboard and Management API. IQueueControl trusts the actor you pass. The HTTP API, dashboard and CLI check permissions first. Next - Rate limits and concurrency: cap how much runs at once. - Workers: pools, fixed and automatic concurrency.

title: Management API
description: The authenticated HTTP API behind the dashboard and the CLI - sign-in, permissions, antiforgery, limits and audit.
body: Runwick.AspNetCore adds an HTTP API for reading and controlling jobs, queues, schedules, capacity and retention. The dashboard and the CLI both go through the same checks, so they share one set of permissions and one audit trail. Setting it up Both AuthenticationSchemes and MapGrants are required. MapRunwickManagement throws at startup when either is missing, or when a named scheme is not registered. There is no anonymous mode and no "localhost only" mode. You bring the sign-in: cookies, OpenID Connect, JWT bearer or anything else ASP.NET Core supports. Runwick does not change your default scheme. It tries the listed schemes in order and never sends a redirect challenge. Permissions MapGrants turns the signed-in user into a list of ManagementGrant values. It runs on every request. Grants never come from the request body or headers. Permission Allows --- --- Jobs.Read Listing and reading jobs (no payloads) Jobs.ReadPayload Revealing a job's payload (audited) Jobs.ReadError Revealing an attempt's error detail (audited) Jobs.Cancel , Jobs.Retry , Jobs.Rerun Job controls Jobs.Dispatch Creating a job from the API or CLI (audited) Queues.Read , Queues.Control Listing queues, pausing and resuming them Schedules.Read , Schedules.Trigger , Schedules.Control , Schedules.Edit Reading, triggering, pausing and resuming, revalidating schedules Capacity.Read , Capacity.Edit Workers and concurrency scopes Settings.Read The host's settings page Retention.Manage Editing the retention policy Audit.Read Reading the audit trail The names are constants on ManagementPermissions . Three presets cover the usual cases: Preset Contains --- --- ManagementRoles.Viewer Jobs.Read , Queues.Read , Schedules.Read , Capacity.Read , Settings.Read ManagementRoles.Operator Viewer, plus cancel, retry, rerun, queue control, schedule trigger and control ManagementRoles.Administrator Operator, plus Schedules.Edit , Capacity.Edit , Retention.Manage Payload, error and audit reads and Jobs.Dispatch are in no preset. Add them on purpose: Scoping to queues Jobs. and Queues. grants can be limited to some queues: Jobs outside the caller's queues answer 404 , exactly like jobs that do not exist, so hidden IDs are never confirmed. Lists are filtered before paging. Schedule, capacity, settings, retention and audit permissions are application-wide; giving them a queue list throws when the grant is built, so a mistake never widens access. Antiforgery Every POST from a browser or a Basic client needs an antiforgery token. Fetch it with GET {prefix}/v1/antiforgery , then send it in the X-Runwick-Antiforgery header: The CLI does this for you. Machine clients A service that calls the API with a bearer token has no cookie, so antiforgery adds nothing. Map the API for machine clients: ForMachineClients() refuses cookie and Basic schemes. If any configured scheme is one of those, it throws at startup. Runwick ships no bearer handler; use your own. Basic authentication For small setups, AddRunwickBasic adds a Basic scheme. You must supply the password check; there are no default credentials. - Requests over plain HTTP are refused. - After 10 failures a minute for one source address and user name, further tries are refused without checking. - Basic counts as a browser scheme, so POST requests still need the antiforgery token. Revisions and command IDs Every control carries the revision the caller last saw, for example "cancel job 42 at generation 1, revision 7". If the target changed in between, the answer is a 409 conflict ( stale revision or stale generation ), not a surprise. Every control also carries a commandId . If a reply is lost, send the same request with the same command ID: the store returns the original result with replayed: true , with no second change and no second audit row. Limits Limits are per process and per signed-in caller. Change them with Configure : ManagementOptions Default --- --- ReadsPerMinute 120 MutationsPerMinute 30 RevealsPerMinute 10 MaxActiveRequests 16 MaxWaitingRequests / MaxWait 32 / 1 s Over a per-caller limit the answer is 429 with Retry-After . When the process is full it is 503 busy . With several replicas, each replica counts on its own. List cursors are protected with ASP.NET Core Data Protection. Replicas that share a key ring accept each other's cursors. Set CursorKey (32 bytes or more) if they do not. Audit Every successful change writes an audit row in the same transaction as the change: who, what, when, the command ID and the reason you passed. Revealing a payload or an error is audited too, and the data is returned only after the audit row is committed. Read the trail with Audit.Read , in the dashboard's Audit page or with runwick audit list . By default the actor is the user's NameIdentifier claim (or Name ), their name, and the scheme used. Override it with .Actor(principal = new ManagementActor(subject, display, scheme)) . Denied requests are not audited. Failed sign-ins are logged (event 1401) with a coarse hash of the source, never the address or user name. A standalone management host The API does not need workers. A small internal web app can serve only the API and the dashboard: This process runs no worker and writes no worker heartbeat. It is also a good place to collect application-wide metrics; see Observability.

title: Cancellation
description: Cancelling a job is a request, not a kill. How the token works, how long Runwick waits, and how to write handlers that stop cleanly.
headings: What happens when you cancel a job
Cancelling from the CLI, dashboard or API
body: Cancellation in Runwick is a request , not a kill. .NET has no safe way to stop code that is already running, and Runwick does not try. It cancels the CancellationToken your handler received and waits for your code to notice. What happens when you cancel a job The job is… What happens --- --- Waiting ( pending or retrying ) It moves to cancelled and never runs. Running The store records "cancel requested". The worker cancels the handler's token. Your code must stop. Already finished Nothing changes. The answer says the job had already finished; it is not reported as a successful cancel. If the handler stops by throwing OperationCanceledException , the run ends as cancelled and is not retried. If the handler finishes successfully before the cancel reaches it, success wins; the history shows both the request and the success. Cancelling from the CLI, dashboard or API runwick jobs cancel-many --file jobs.jsonl cancels up to 100 jobs at once. In C , use IJobControl from Runwick.Management : The target carries the generation and revision you last saw. If the job changed in between, you get a conflict rather than cancelling something you did not look at. A rejection comes back as a result with a Code , not as an exception. The dashboard, CLI and API show "cancel requested" until the worker reports how the run ended. They never claim a cancel "stopped the handler". One token, four causes The same token is cancelled for four different reasons: Cause When --- --- UserRequested Someone cancelled the job. Timeout The job's ExecutionTimeout ran out. See Retries and timeouts. Shutdown The worker is stopping. LeaseLost The worker could not renew its lease in time and no longer owns the job. IJobContext.CancellationCauses is a flags value that tells you which ones Runwick has seen. More than one can be set. Rethrow rather than swallow. Runwick classifies the run from the causes: Cause Outcome --- --- Timeout Timed out. Retryable. User request Cancelled. Not retried. Shutdown Interrupted. Retryable, and picked up again after restart. Lease lost The worker writes no result. The store's recovery decides once the lease expires. An OperationCanceledException that is not caused by any of these, for example your own HttpClient timeout, is an ordinary retryable failure. Write handlers that cooperate Give ct to every database call, HTTP call and Task.Delay . Most .NET APIs stop promptly when it is cancelled. If a step cannot be interrupted, keep it well under the grace period. A cancelled or interrupted run may have done part of its work. A retried run starts from the top. See Delivery guarantees. Grace period After the first user, timeout or shutdown cancellation, Runwick waits up to CancellationGrace (default 10 seconds) for the handler to return. Repeated signals do not restart the clock. - Handler returns within grace: the worker cleans up the DI scope and records the outcome normally. - Handler ignores the token: after the grace period the worker stops renewing the lease and writes no result. The code keeps running in the process, holding its pool slot and DI scope until it actually returns. When the lease expires, the store's recovery closes the attempt: cancelled if a cancel was requested, otherwise retried or failed by the usual budget. Another worker may then run the job while the old code is still going. Worker timings are checked against each other at startup; see Configuration. Concurrency limits count valid leases, not code that is still physically running. If overlap would be harmful, honour the token and use fencing tokens. Shutdown When the host stops, the worker stops claiming new jobs and lets running handlers finish. After the drain phase (15 seconds by default) it cancels the remaining handlers with cause Shutdown , gives them a few seconds, then records what it knows. The whole shutdown budget is 25 seconds by default, inside .NET's usual 30-second host shutdown timeout. Keep the host's timeout above Runwick's. See Workers and Deployment. Cancelling a dispatch call The token you pass to DispatchAsync is different. It only stops waiting for the store; it never cancels a job the store has accepted. See Dispatching. Next - Job context - Retries and timeouts

title: Workers
description: Run jobs with AddWorker - pools, queues, concurrency, leases, shutdown and recovery after a crash.
body: A worker is any process that calls AddWorker . It claims jobs from the store, runs your handlers and writes the results back. The same process can also dispatch, run the scheduler or serve the dashboard. A process without AddWorker only produces jobs and never runs a handler. Adding a worker AddWorker may be called once per application. A worker needs at least one pool, and pool names must be unique. Startup fails with a clear configuration error if any of these rules is broken. Pools A pool is a group of slots (tickets) that share a set of queues. A job needs a free ticket before the worker claims it, and the ticket comes back only when the job has finished and its result is stored. That is what keeps memory bounded when the store is slow or away. Use more than one pool when some work must not starve other work. In the example above, a flood of reports can never take the slots that emails need. Method What it does --- --- Queues("a", "b") Subscribes to queues, each with weight 1 Queue("a", weight) Subscribes to one queue with a weight from 1 to 1,000. Higher weight means a larger share of claims FixedConcurrency(n) A fixed number of tickets. This is the default, with 4 AutoConcurrency(min, max) Lets the pool grow and shrink between min and max LaneSelection(mode) Weighted (default), StrictWithAging or Strict LaneWeights(high, medium, low) Shares of the priority lanes. Default 6 : 3 : 1 Rules checked at startup: - Every queue a pool names must be used by a registered job or declared with runwick.Queue("name") . - A pool subscribes to at least one queue, and to each queue only once. - A pool is either fixed or automatic, never both. - The sum of every pool's maximum must not exceed MaxOutstandingAttempts , which is 16 by default. How priorities and lanes interact is explained in Queues and priorities. Automatic concurrency AutoConcurrency(min, max) adjusts the pool's ticket count from how busy the tickets are and from the pool's share of waiting work. It moves carefully: it needs several samples in a row before it grows or shrinks, waits between changes, and never changes by more than a quarter at a time. It stops growing when the store looks unhealthy. Shrinking never cancels running work; it only stops refilling slots. The automatic controller scales the slots of this process only. It does not start containers or coordinate with other replicas. To scale out, export the metrics (see Observability) and let your platform add instances. Leases When a worker claims a job it gets a lease : ownership with an expiry time decided by the store's clock. The worker renews the lease in the background while the handler runs. Every write the worker makes carries a token from the claim, so a worker that lost its lease cannot overwrite the result of whoever took over. WorkerOptions Default Meaning --- --- --- LeaseDuration 60 s Length of each lease LeaseSafetyMargin 10 s The worker stops trusting a lease this long before the store would expire it RenewalInterval / RenewalJitter 15 s / 3 s Renewal runs every 12 to 18 s MinimumInvocationMargin 15 s A handler does not start unless at least this much lease time is left ControlRequestTimeout 5 s Longest wait for one store call on the ownership path CancellationGrace 10 s Time a cancelled handler gets to return CleanupBudget 10 s Time allowed for disposing the job's DI scope Change them with Configure : The timings depend on each other. Runwick checks the rules at startup and refuses a configuration that breaks them; it never quietly adjusts a value. The full list is in Configuration. If a renewal is not confirmed in time, the worker treats the lease as lost for good. It cancels the handler's CancellationToken , stops renewing, and never writes a result for that attempt, even if a late reply arrives. .NET has no safe way to kill a running method. A handler that ignores its token keeps running while another worker may already run the same job. Handlers must be safe to run more than once. See Delivery guarantees. Shutdown When the host stops, the worker shuts down in steps, measured from the moment the stop began: No new jobs are claimed. This happens at once. Running handlers keep going. Their leases are still renewed and their results are still written. Every handler still running has its CancellationToken cancelled and gets a few seconds to return. Known results are written. At 25 s the worker stops talking to the store. Anything still open is left to lease expiry and recovery by another worker. WorkerOptions Default --- --- ShutdownDrain 15 s ShutdownCancellation 5 s ShutdownFinalization 5 s ShutdownBudget 25 s (the three slices must fit inside it) The .NET host gives hosted services 30 seconds to stop by default. Keep it above Runwick's 25 seconds, and keep your container platform's grace period above the host's: If the host kills the process early, nothing is corrupted, but jobs still running wait for their leases to expire before another worker picks them up. When a worker crashes Every worker runs a recovery loop, by default every 5 seconds (give or take 1 second, RecoveryScanInterval and RecoveryScanJitter ). It finds jobs whose lease has expired and puts them back: - The handler had started. The attempt is closed as abandoned. The job retries if it has executions left, and otherwise fails. If someone asked to cancel it meanwhile, it ends as cancelled. - The handler had not started yet. The worker claimed the job but died before running it. This does not use up one of the job's executions. It is counted separately (5 times in a row by default, with short delays from 1 s to 30 s), so a job that crashes every worker before it starts still stops eventually. There is one small gap: the store records "this execution started" just before calling your handler. A crash in that instant still costs an execution. Resource usage per attempt WorkerOptions.RecordResourceUsage is on by default. The worker records CPU time, allocated bytes and working set for each attempt and stores them with it, so the dashboard can show them. The measured cost is a few microseconds per attempt. Set it to false to turn it off. Other work a worker does - It publishes a heartbeat ("worker X is alive, listening to these queues"), which the dashboard and runwick workers list show. - It runs the cleanup loop for old records. See Retention. - It reports a worker readiness check. See Health checks.

title: PostgreSQL
description: Run Runwick on PostgreSQL 16, 17 or 18, create its schema with a migration role, and stage jobs in your own transactions.
headings: Roles: migration role and runtime role
Create a job in your own transaction
body: PostgreSQL is Runwick's reference store. The rest of Runwick is measured against it. Producers and workers can run on many hosts, as long as they all connect to the same primary. It is also the store where a job can share a transaction with your own data. Requirements Item Requirement --- --- Server PostgreSQL 16, 17 or 18 (18 is the reference) Database UTF8 encoding, standard conforming strings = on (the default) Extensions None Topology Connect directly to the primary Package Runwick.Postgres (uses Npgsql) The migration checks the server version and encoding before it writes anything, and stops with a clear error if they do not match. Install Create the schema Runwick never changes the schema when your application starts. You run the migration as a separate deployment step, from code or from the command line: The migration is safe to run again: a fully applied migration is a no-op. Two runners at once do not collide, because the runner holds a PostgreSQL advisory lock for the whole run. It waits up to 60 seconds for that lock. If it fails, it throws PostgresMigrationException , whose Code says what went wrong (for example server version unsupported or migration lock unavailable ). The CLI never takes a connection string as an argument, because command lines are visible to other users of the machine. Pass the name of an environment variable ( --connection-env ) or pipe it in ( --connection-stdin ). Use the CLI version that matches your Runwick packages: it installs the migrations compiled into it. Roles: migration role and runtime role Use two database roles: - Migration role. Creates and owns the runwick schema. It runs MigrateAsync , and the store administration commands ( runwick store status , store admission , store activate-capability , store reidentify ). - Runtime role. Used by your application. It needs data access to the tables in the runwick schema, and no DDL rights. Runwick does not create database roles or grant privileges for you. Grant the runtime role access with your usual tooling after the migration has run. Schedules and rate limits need a capability raised once per application, with the migration role: runwick store activate-capability --name scheduler --application my-app --provider postgres --connection-env RUNWICK MIGRATE CONN . Use --name rate admission for rate limits. See Schedules and Upgrades. Register the store UsePostgres takes the connection string and an optional Action . Runwick creates and owns its own Npgsql data sources, and never logs the connection string. Option Default Notes --- --- --- PostgresOptions.Schema runwick Only runwick is supported in this release. Any other value is refused at startup. An empty connection string fails at startup with missing store . Connections Runwick keeps separate connection pools for lease work (claim, renew, finish) and for everything else, so a burst of dispatches cannot starve lease renewals. With default settings, plan for about 23 connections per worker process: 8 for lease work, 14 for other work and 1 for the listener described below. A process that only dispatches opens no lease-work pool. Raising ProducerOptions.MaxConcurrentCalls adds the same number of connections. Add your own business connections on top when you size max connections . How workers notice new jobs Workers poll for due work. On PostgreSQL, a committed dispatch also sends a NOTIFY on a dedicated listener connection, so idle workers wake up sooner. The notification is only a hint. If it is lost, polling still finds the job. Primary only Ownership decisions (who holds a job's lease) are never read from a replica. Point every Runwick process at the primary. Connection poolers such as PgBouncer, proxies, and failover setups have not been tested with Runwick. If you use one, you are outside what has been tested. In particular, do not route Runwick through anything that could send a query to a replica. Create a job in your own transaction When your business tables and Runwick's tables are in the same database, you can create a job in the same transaction as your own rows. Inject IPostgresJobDispatcher and call StageAsync with your open NpgsqlTransaction : StageAsync returns a StagedDispatch , not a DispatchReceipt . Nothing is durable until you commit. Runwick never commits, rolls back or retries your transaction. If the transaction fails with a serialization error or a deadlock, retrying the whole transaction is your job. StageManyAsync stages a batch of up to 100 jobs the same way. The other direction works too: a handler can mark its job as succeeded inside your transaction. Transactions covers both, with their rules and limits. What PostgreSQL does not promise - No high availability. A failover or a restored backup is a break in history: receipts, uniqueness windows and fences from before it are not guaranteed to carry over. - Delivery is still at-least-once. A handler can run more than once. See Delivery guarantees. - Durability is what your server's settings give you. A confirmed dispatch means PostgreSQL committed it. Runwick does not check synchronous commit ; keep it on (the default), or a crash can lose writes that were already confirmed. Next steps Stage jobs and complete them inside your own transaction. Migrate, drain and roll back safely. Process shapes, shutdown timing and connection budgets.

title: Configuration
description: Every default in one place, for jobs, workers, producers, stores, retention, the scheduler, the outbox relay and the fixed limits.
body: All configuration goes through AddRunwick(runwick = ...) and the store, outbox and management extensions. Times are as written. Runwick checks every value at startup and refuses a configuration it cannot run safely. It never quietly adjusts a value for you. Per job Set per job with an attribute or the fluent builder, or for all jobs with runwick.JobDefaults(...) . Later layers win: library default, then JobDefaults , then attribute, then fluent. Setting Default Attribute / fluent --- --- --- Queue default [Queue("emails")] / .ToQueue("emails") Priority medium ( low , medium , high ) [Priority("high")] / .WithPriority("high") Maximum executions (counts real starts, so 3 means two automatic retries) 3 [MaxExecutions(5)] / .WithMaxExecutions(5) Execution timeout none .WithExecutionTimeout(...) / .WithoutExecutionTimeout() Retry delay (exponential, half random) 5 s first, never more than 60 s .WithRetryDelay(initial, max) Re-queue after a worker took a job but never started it up to 5 times .WithMaxUnstartedAbandonments(n) Delay between those re-queues 1 s growing to 30 s .WithUnstartedRecoveryDelay(initial, max) Uniqueness, rate limits, concurrency limits off until you declare them .UniqueWhileActive(...) , .RollingWindow(...) , .MaxConcurrent(...) and others With the defaults, the first retry waits between 2.5 and 5 seconds, the second between 5 and 10. See Retries and timeouts. Worker: WorkerOptions Set with runwick.AddWorker(w = w.Configure(o = ...)) . Most apps never touch these. They are tied together; see Startup validation. Option Default What it does --- --- --- LeaseDuration 60 s How long a claim on a job lasts before it must be renewed LeaseSafetyMargin 10 s The worker treats the lease as expired this much early RenewalInterval / RenewalJitter 15 s / 3 s Renew every 12 to 18 s LeaseWatchdogInterval 1 s How often the safety watchdog checks leases (at most 1 s) SchedulerAllowance 2 s Allowance for timer lag ControlRequestTimeout 5 s Longest wait for one claim, renew or finish call ControlRetryInitialBackoff / ControlRetryMaxBackoff 100 ms / 1 s Backoff between retries of those calls MinimumInvocationMargin 15 s Lease time that must be left to start a handler ClaimResolutionBudget / BeginResolutionBudget 15 s / 15 s How long to resolve an uncertain claim or start CompletionResolutionBudget 30 s How long to resolve an uncertain finish CancellationGrace 10 s Time a cancelled handler gets to exit CleanupBudget 10 s Time for the attempt's scope to dispose OwnershipCommandLifetime 30 s Deadline of each claim, renew or finish command RecoveryScanInterval / RecoveryScanJitter 5 s / 1 s Scan for jobs of crashed workers every 4 to 6 s ShutdownBudget 25 s Total time for Runwick's shutdown ShutdownDrain / ShutdownCancellation / ShutdownFinalization 15 s / 5 s / 5 s The three shutdown stages; their sum must fit in ShutdownBudget RecordResourceUsage true Store CPU time, allocations and working set per attempt Keep the host's shutdown timeout ( HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout , 30 s by default in .NET) above ShutdownBudget . Runwick does not change it for you. Pools Setting Default Notes --- --- --- Pool size fixed 4 .FixedConcurrency(n) with n at least 1, or .AutoConcurrency(min, max) ; not both Queue weight 1 .Queue(name, weight) , 1 to 1,000 Lane selection Weighted .LaneSelection(...) : Weighted , StrictWithAging or Strict Lane weights high : medium : low 6 : 3 : 1 .LaneWeights(h, m, l) ; a waiting lane ages after 60 s Most jobs one worker holds at once 16 w.MaxOutstandingAttempts(n) ; the sum of pool maximums must fit Producer: ProducerOptions Set with runwick.Producer(o = ...) . Option Default Notes --- --- --- MaxConcurrentCalls 8 Dispatch calls in flight at once; at least 1. On PostgreSQL, raising it adds connections. MaxWaitingOperations 64 Callers waiting for a slot; more fail with local capacity exceeded without sending anything AdmissionWait 1 s Longest wait for a slot CommandLifetime 5 min How long a prepared dispatch stays valid; also the maximum Stores Option Default Allowed --- --- --- PostgresOptions.Schema runwick only runwick SqliteOptions.WriterBusyTimeout 2 s 100 ms to 30 s SqliteOptions.ReaderThreads 2 1 to 8 RedisOptions.ProfileRecheckInterval 30 s 5 s to 5 min See PostgreSQL, SQLite and Redis. Retention Cleanup runs in worker processes. Its budgets are set with w.Retention(r = ...) : RetentionOptions Default Allowed --- --- --- Enabled true BatchRows 100 1 to 1,000 BatchDetailBytes 1 MiB 64 KiB to 16 MiB BatchTarget 500 ms 50 ms to 2 s BatchPause 1 s 0 to 60 s IdlePoll 60 s 1 s to 1 h How long records are kept is a stored policy per application, edited through the management API. The defaults: Record Kept for --- --- Detail of succeeded jobs 7 days Detail of failed jobs 30 days Job history 90 days Audit 90 days Scaling events 7 days Schedule occurrences 30 days Worker presence 24 hours Cleanup is bounded work, not a promise to keep up with any load. Deleting rows does not erase backups or copies. See Retention. Scheduler: SchedulerOptions Set with runwick.AddScheduler(o = ...) . The scheduler needs the scheduler capability raised once per application, or startup fails with scheduler not active . Option Default --- --- PollInterval 1 s while work is due IdlePollInterval 5 s when idle (15 s on PostgreSQL while its listener is healthy) JobsPerSecond / Burst 100 / 32 per scheduler process Per schedule: misfire policy RunOnce with 60 s grace (up to 24 h); catch-up at most 1,000 jobs per episode and 7 days back. See Schedules. Outbox relay: OutboxRelayOptions Option Default Allowed --- --- --- Enabled true MaxInFlight 4 1 to 64 LeaseDuration / RenewalInterval 60 s / 15 s lease at least 5 s and at least 3 renewals ProviderCallTimeout 5 s shorter than RenewalInterval IdlePoll 1 s positive RetryInitial / RetryMax 1 s / 60 s TransportLifetime 30 s at most 30 s Acceptance horizon (per message, OutboxStageOptions ) 7 days up to 30 days See Outbox. Telemetry: RunwickTelemetryOptions Set with runwick.Telemetry(o = ...) . Option Default Allowed --- --- --- RecordExceptionDetails false Puts a cleaned, bounded exception message on spans and logs MaxSeriesPerInstrument 1,000 100 to 10,000 CollectApplicationMetrics false Makes this process the application-wide metrics collector ApplicationSamplePeriod 15 s 5 s to 5 min CollectorName default Management and dashboard Management needs authentication schemes and a grant mapping, or it does not start. There is no anonymous mode. The dashboard title defaults to Runwick . See Management API and Dashboard. Fixed limits These cannot be configured. Limit Value --- --- Serialized payload 1 MiB of JSON, 32 levels deep Application, queue and pool names 1 to 128 characters, [A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9. -] Job names 1 to 200 characters, same characters Uniqueness and resource keys 1 to 512 bytes of UTF-8 Business metadata 16 KiB and 32 entries Batch dispatch 100 items or 2 MiB Rate limit 1 to 100,000 per window; window 1 s to 24 h; at most 8 rate scopes per job Startup validation When the host starts, Runwick checks the whole configuration and throws RunwickConfigurationException listing every problem at once. Each entry has a code, the setting it is about, and the rule it broke. Timing problems have the code invalid timing : The worker timings must satisfy these rules. The defaults pass all of them: Rule With defaults --- --- Every duration is positive and a whole number of milliseconds ( RenewalJitter and RecoveryScanJitter may be 0) pass LeaseSafetyMargin is less than LeaseDuration 10 s 0 (RenewalInterval + RenewalJitter) + 2 × ControlRequestTimeout + ControlRetryMaxBackoff + SchedulerAllowance is less than LeaseDuration − LeaseSafetyMargin 31 s Setting LeaseDuration to 30 s on its own fails: 31 s of renewal path does not fit in 20 s of usable lease. Raising ControlRequestTimeout to 10 s fails too, because the start margin then needs 23 s. If you change one timing, scale the related ones with it, for example a 120 s lease with a 20 s safety margin and a 30 s renewal interval. Other startup errors you may see: invalid pool (for example a pool that subscribes a queue no job or Queue(...) call registers), pool without queue , pool budget exceeded (pool maximums add up to more than the worker's limit), invalid policy for store options, and missing store when no store is configured. Troubleshooting lists the common ones.

title: Redis
description: Run Runwick on one durable Redis primary with append-only fsync on every write, and know the limits that come with it.
body: The Redis store keeps Runwick's data on one Redis primary that writes every change to its append-only file and syncs it to disk before it replies. Producers and workers can run on many hosts. Job behaviour is the same as on PostgreSQL: the same states, retries, receipts, uniqueness and rate rules. Redis is only safe for jobs with the right server settings, so Runwick checks them before it starts and keeps checking while it runs. Requirements Item Requirement --- --- Server Redis 8.2 or newer Topology One standalone primary. No Cluster, no Sentinel. Persistence AOF with appendfsync always (see below) Package Runwick.Redis (uses StackExchange.Redis) Server configuration Start Redis with these settings. Runwick refuses to run with anything else: Setting Why --- --- appendonly yes , appendfsync always Every write is on disk before Redis replies, so a confirmed job survives a crash. no-appendfsync-on-rewrite no Keeps fsync on while the AOF is being rewritten. maxmemory-policy noeviction Redis must never drop keys to free memory. A full server returns errors instead. aof-load-truncated no A damaged AOF stops Redis at startup instead of quietly loading less data. Size maxmemory with room to spare. With noeviction , a full server refuses writes, and dispatches fail until you free space. Runwick reads the settings with CONFIG GET and MODULE LIST . If an ACL blocks either, the value counts as unverifiable and the store refuses to run. Restrict CONFIG SET with ACLs if you need to, but leave CONFIG GET and MODULE LIST allowed for Runwick's user. Do not remove CONFIG with rename-command . Managed Redis services that hide CONFIG are not supported. Install and migrate Write the store's identity once before the first start: Running it again does nothing if the store is already installed. Without it, the app refuses to start because the store is not installed. Register the store The configuration string is a StackExchange.Redis string. Runwick uses only the endpoint, credentials, TLS settings, defaultDatabase and connectTimeout from it, and never logs it. Several endpoints, or a Sentinel service name, are refused at startup with topology unsupported . Option Default Allowed What it does --- --- --- --- ProfileRecheckInterval 30 s 5 s to 5 min How often the settings and topology check runs while the app runs. What Runwick checks At startup, on every reconnect and every ProfileRecheckInterval , Runwick checks on a separate connection: - the five settings above, through CONFIG GET ; - through INFO : role:master , redis mode:standalone , cluster enabled:0 , AOF enabled, the last AOF write succeeded, and the version is at least 8.2; - through MODULE LIST : the loaded modules, which are reported but allowed. When A failed check means --- --- At startup The app does not start. The error names the setting and the value it saw, for example appendfsync=everysec . While running Runwick stops sending new work: no new claims, dispatches or schedule runs. Health reports the store as unhealthy ( store profile mismatch ) until a later check passes. Calls already sent finish as usual. Replicas attached to the primary are allowed and reported. But a replica promoted to primary is a different history, and Runwick does not follow a failover. History checks Each process remembers the store's identity and the highest revision it has seen for the application. If Redis comes back empty (for example after FLUSHALL ), with another store's identity, or with a lower revision, Runwick stops admitting work and treats every lease it held as lost. It does not resume until you restart the process against an intact store. This check catches a history that went backwards. It cannot prove that no write was lost. One application, one hash slot Every key of an application starts with rw:{ }: , so all of them live in one hash slot. That is what lets one Lua script change a job's records together. Several applications can share one Redis database. The cost: one application's throughput is bounded by one Redis server thread, and one very large command (for example a big batch) delays every other command of that application while it runs. If one application needs more, split the work into separate applications. No transactions with your data Redis cannot join your business database's transaction. There is no StageAsync and no transactional completion on Redis. To create a job only when your business data commits, write it to an outbox in your business database; the relay delivers it to the Redis store. Polling There are no wake-up notifications between processes. Workers find new jobs by polling. Within one process, a commit wakes that process's own workers. What Redis does not promise - No high availability. Failover, Sentinel promotion and Cluster are not supported. A promoted replica may have lost acknowledged jobs. - Durability is the primary's disk and appendfsync always . Restoring an AOF or RDB file is a break in history. - Running Redis without appendfsync always is not a supported configuration, even for benchmarks. - Results on Redis say nothing about speed compared with PostgreSQL. Next steps Commit a job with your business data, then deliver it to Redis. See the store's status in your health endpoint.

title: Job context
description: Read facts about the current run with IJobContext, log with them, and wrap runs in middleware.
body: IJobContext gives a handler read-only facts about the run it is in: the job ID, which run this is, the queue, metadata, schedule and more. Inject it into the handler's constructor. It is not a HandleAsync argument, so handlers that do not need it simply leave it out. There is one context per run. It can only be resolved inside the run's DI scope; resolving it anywhere else throws InvalidOperationException . What it exposes Identity Property Meaning --- --- Application The application name. JobId The job's permanent ID. Stable across retries and manual retries. AttemptId The ID of this one attempt. New on every try. JobName The stored job name, for example email.welcome . CreatedAt When the store created the job. Runs and budget Property Meaning --- --- ExecutionNumber Which run this is within the current generation, from 1. MaxExecutions The run budget for this generation. Generation 1 for the original dispatch. A manual retry or rerun starts generation 2, 3 and so on, each with a fresh budget. ExecutionNumber == MaxExecutions means this is the last automatic try. You might log louder, or send a different alert, on that run. Routing and payload Property Meaning --- --- Queue , Priority Where the job was routed. OriginalPayloadVersion The version of the stored bytes. CurrentPayloadVersion The version handed to the handler after upgrades. SerializerProfileId , SerializerProfileVersion runwick.json , 1. GetPayload () The same upgraded payload the handler received. Useful in middleware. TJob must be the registered current type. Metadata, tracing and fences Property Meaning --- --- Metadata Business metadata passed at dispatch, such as a tenant. Trace The W3C traceparent and tracestate captured at dispatch. Fences One fencing token per capacity-1 resource scope this run holds. See Rate limits and concurrency. Schedule The schedule occurrence that created this job, or null . CancellationCauses Which cancellation causes Runwick has seen. See Cancellation. Items A per-run dictionary for passing data between middleware and the handler. Never saved. Everything except Items and CancellationCauses stays the same for the whole run. Scheduled jobs For a job created by a schedule, Schedule holds: Property Meaning --- --- ScheduleName The schedule key. ScheduledAt The occurrence this job belongs to. CoveredFrom , CoveredUntil The time range the job covers. After a missed run with the RunOnce policy, one job can cover several occurrences. What it does not expose The context is read-only by design. It has no database connection, no lease, no way to extend the lease or the timeout, and no progress reporting . Lease renewal is done by the worker, not the handler, so a handler cannot keep a job alive forever. If you need to report progress, write it to your own table or cache keyed by JobId . Logging Runwick does not add a logging scope for you. Inject ILogger as usual and include the IDs you need: When tracing is on, each run gets a process {queue} span, and the handler runs inside a runwick.execute child span. Spans your own code starts become its children, and the run is linked to the dispatch that created it. See Observability. Middleware Middleware wraps every run, like ASP.NET Core middleware wraps a request. It receives the same context and token as the handler: A middleware either calls next() exactly once and returns its result, or returns a result without calling it. Calling next() twice, or returning while it is still running, is a contract fault and fails the job permanently. Result Meaning --- --- JobExecutionResult.Succeeded() Success. Return it explicitly if you skip the handler on purpose. JobExecutionResult.Retry(reason, delay) Retryable failure. Costs one run. JobExecutionResult.Failed(code, message) Permanent failure. JobExecutionResult.Cancelled(reason) Ends the job as cancelled. Register middleware globally, per job, or by alias so that a contracts assembly can name middleware without referencing its code: The order, outer to inner, is: global middleware in registration order, then attribute aliases by Order (ties by alias name), then fluent per-job middleware, then the handler. Middleware is scoped and resolved fresh for every run. A worker that sees an alias nobody registered refuses to start ( unknown middleware alias ); a producer-only app does not check aliases. Middleware cannot extend leases, reset budgets or finish a job itself. Those are the worker's job. Next - Retries and timeouts - Testing: run handlers without a database.

title: Dispatching
description: Create jobs with IJobDispatcher, set queue, priority, start time and metadata, dispatch in batches, and handle an unknown outcome.
body: Dispatching writes a job to the store. Inject IJobDispatcher (a singleton) anywhere in your app: DispatchAsync returns only after the store has confirmed the write. There is no "fire and forget" mode. The job's type must be registered (see Jobs and handlers). Runwick looks it up by the object's runtime type. The receipt DispatchAsync returns a DispatchReceipt : Property Meaning --- --- JobId The job's permanent ID. It stays the same across retries. OperationId The ID of this dispatch command. Disposition Created for a new job, or Reused when a uniqueness key matched an existing job. DuplicateMatch Which key matched: None , Active , Window or ActiveAndWindow . PolicyDrift true when a reused job was created under a different retry or timeout policy than the current one. ConfirmedAcknowledgementProfile The durability rule the store confirmed, for example postgres.synchronous-commit . A receipt tells you which job it is. It is not a status snapshot: a reused job may already have finished. Dispatch options Pass a DispatchOptions to change one dispatch. Every property is optional. Option What it does --- --- Queue Sends the job to another registered queue. An unknown queue fails with unknown queue . Priority low , medium or high . Raises or lowers the job's declared priority. NotBefore The earliest time the job may start. Uniqueness Active and window keys. See Uniqueness. Metadata Business metadata such as a tenant. The handler reads it from IJobContext.Metadata . Delayed jobs NotBefore is a lower bound, not an exact start time. The job waits in pending until that instant and then becomes eligible like any other job. It starts when a worker has a free slot. A time in the past means "eligible now". The value is rounded up to the next millisecond. There is no separate "schedule" call for one-off delays. For repeating work, use Schedules. Metadata rules - Keys use the name grammar ( A-Z a-z 0-9 . - , up to 128 characters). Values must be valid text without control characters. - At most 32 entries and 16 KiB in total. - Metadata is part of what a window key compares, so the same key with different metadata is a conflict. Runwick also captures the current trace context ( traceparent , tracestate ) at dispatch, so the run is linked to the request that created it. Batch dispatch DispatchManyAsync dispatches up to 100 jobs in one store transaction: - Every item is created (or reused) or none is. - Items has one result per input, in input order ( Ordinal is the 0-based index). - The limits are 100 items and 2 MiB for the whole batch. Split larger inputs yourself. - If any item is invalid, the whole batch is rejected before anything is written. The DispatchValidationException lists every bad ordinal in ItemFailures . - Duplicates inside one batch resolve as if dispatched one after another: a later item that matches an earlier one is Reused . By default a uniqueness conflict in any item fails the whole batch with UniquenessConflictException . Set ContinueOnConflict to commit the other items and report the conflicts per item: Errors Every Runwick exception has a stable Code and a Disposition . The disposition answers "did anything get written?": Disposition Meaning --- --- KnownNotApplied Nothing was written. It is safe to fix the input and try again. OutcomeUnknown The write may or may not have happened. Common cases: Exception Code Disposition --- --- --- DispatchValidationException for example payload too large , invalid key known not applied UniquenessConflictException uniqueness conflict , uniqueness composition conflict known not applied LocalCapacityExceededException local capacity exceeded known not applied, never sent StoreUnavailableException store unavailable known not applied DispatchOutcomeUnknownException outcome unknown unknown DispatchCanceledAfterSendException cancelled after send unknown When the outcome is unknown A network failure after the command was sent leaves Runwick unable to say whether the store committed it. It does not guess. It throws an exception with Disposition == ErrorDisposition.OutcomeUnknown that carries the OperationId and, when available, the prepared request. You have three honest options: The exception's Prepared property holds the exact request. Sending it again through IPreparedJobDispatcher is safe: the store recognises the operation ID and returns the original receipt instead of creating a second job. IPreparedJobDispatcher.ResolveAsync(operationId) returns Confirmed (with the receipt), NotObserved , Recovering or ExpiredUnknown . NotObserved is not proof the write failed: the original command may still be running. If the dispatch had a window key, dispatching again with the same key and payload returns the same job. A plain second DispatchAsync is a new operation. Without a uniqueness key it can create a second job. A prepared request is valid for 5 minutes by default ( ProducerOptions.CommandLifetime ). After that the store guarantees it will never apply it, and re-sending it gives a definite answer ( command expired ) for 24 hours more. Cancellation The CancellationToken only stops waiting . It never cancels a job the store has accepted. Cancelled before the command was sent, you get a plain OperationCanceledException (nothing written). Cancelled after, you get DispatchCanceledAfterSendException , which means the outcome is unknown. Prepared dispatch IPreparedJobDispatcher splits dispatch into two steps. Prepare validates and serializes the job and fixes its operation ID and deadline without touching the store. DispatchAsync(prepared) sends it, as many times as you need. Export() turns a prepared request into bytes you can store and ImportPrepared(bytes) reads them back. The bytes contain the payload unencrypted, so keep them out of logs. Producer limits Each process limits how many dispatch calls it sends at once, so a burst cannot exhaust the database connection pool. Configure them with runwick.Producer(...) : The values above are the defaults. When all slots are busy and the wait runs out, or too many callers are already waiting, the call fails at once with LocalCapacityExceededException . Nothing was sent, so it is safe to retry later. A batch counts as one call. Dispatch works while a queue is paused. Pausing only stops workers from picking jobs up. Next - Uniqueness: stop duplicate jobs. - Transactions: create a job in the same transaction as your own data. - Outbox: dispatch reliably to a different store.

title: Schedules
description: Create jobs on a cron timetable or at one fixed time, handle missed runs and daylight saving, and pause or trigger a schedule.
headings: Turn on the scheduler capability first
At most one job per occurrence
body: A schedule turns "every night at 02:00" into ordinary jobs. The scheduler only creates jobs; workers run them like any other job, with the same retries, limits and guarantees. Turn on the scheduler capability first Schedules need the store capability scheduler , raised once per application. Until then, startup fails with scheduler not active , and the error message names the command to run. This registers the application in the store. The first start fails at the scheduler; that is expected. Use --provider sqlite or --provider redis for the other stores. From code: RunwickPostgresMigrations.ActivateCapabilityAsync(connectionString, "my-app", "scheduler", "deploy") , or the same method on RunwickSqliteMigrations and RunwickRedisMigrations . This is done once per application and cannot be undone. Older Runwick binaries that do not know the capability can no longer create jobs for that application afterwards. Where the scheduler runs AddScheduler() runs the scheduler role in this process. You can run it in as many processes as you like. There is no leader election: each occurrence has a unique key in the store, so only one process can create its job. AddSchedule without AddScheduler in the same process is allowed. The schedule is then registered the first time a process that runs the scheduler and declares it starts. The values above are the defaults. AddScheduler may be called once. Defining a schedule AddSchedule(key, job) takes a key and the job instance to create on each occurrence. The payload is frozen when the schedule is registered. The job type must be registered. Each key may be declared once. Every schedule has exactly one of Cron or Once ( schedule definition missing otherwise). Cron Format Fields --- --- FiveField (default) minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week SixField second, minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week Each field takes , a value, a range a-b , a step /n or a-b/n , or a comma list of those. Months accept JAN – DEC and days of week SUN – SAT ; Sunday is 0 or 7. Not supported: macros such as @daily , ? , L , W , , H , year fields and TZ= prefixes. An expression is at most 256 characters. When both day of month and day of week are restricted, a date matches if either matches. 0 9 1 MON runs at 09:00 on the 1st of every month and on every Monday. Time zones Without a zone, schedules run in UTC. A zone must be an IANA ID such as Europe/Berlin . Windows IDs and Local are refused. Runwick ships a pinned copy of the time-zone database, so a server's OS update cannot silently move a schedule. Daylight saving needs two decisions: Option Values --- --- OnGap Skip (default), Shift OnFold Earlier (default), Later , Both Once After its one occurrence the schedule is finished. For a single delayed job you usually want DispatchOptions.NotBefore instead; see Dispatching. At most one job per occurrence Each occurrence, such as "02:00 on 5 March", creates at most one job .
