The job it creates is at-least-once like every job, so its handler can still run more than once. Make it safe to repeat. When a schedule is first registered, the first occurrence is the first one after that moment. There is no backfill of earlier times. The handler can read which occurrence it belongs to from IJobContext.Schedule . See Job context. Missed occurrences If no scheduler was running when an occurrence was due, and it is now more than the grace period late (default 60 seconds), the misfire policy decides: Policy What happens --- --- RunOnce (default) One job now, recorded as covering the whole missed range. Skip No job. The skipped range is recorded. CatchUp One job per missed occurrence, oldest first, in small paced batches. Grace can be 0 to 24 hours. Catch-up stops at 1,000 jobs per episode by default (1 to 10,000) and refuses occurrences older than 7 days by default (1 minute to 31 days). When it hits either limit it creates no more jobs and flags the schedule as needing review, rather than silently dropping occurrences. Overlap By default a new occurrence's job can run while the previous one is still running. Serialize adds a capacity-1 concurrency scope shared by the schedule's jobs, so only one runs at a time. It does not stop jobs being created: if each run takes longer than the interval, jobs queue up. Options for the created jobs WithOptions sets the queue, priority, metadata and active uniqueness of every job the schedule creates: - NotBefore is refused ( schedule delay unsupported ). - Window uniqueness is refused ( schedule window unsupported ). - An active key makes every occurrence share one key, so it requires .AllowOccurrenceReuse() ( schedule occurrence reuse required ). An occurrence that finds the key held is linked to the existing job instead of creating a new one. Changing a schedule in code Registration never overwrites. If you change a schedule's cron, zone, payload or options in code and redeploy, the scheduler logs a warning that the stored definition differs, and the stored definition stays in effect . Pause and enabled state are never reset by a restart either. There is no public operation to edit a stored schedule in this release. To change timing, declare the new definition under a new key and pause the old one. Pausing, resuming and triggering Pausing a schedule stops it creating jobs. Jobs it already created are not paused or cancelled. On resume you choose what happens to occurrences missed while paused: SkipPaused , RunOnce or CatchUp . Trigger creates one extra job now, even while the schedule is paused. It never moves the timetable. The trigger ID is an idempotency key: the same ID returns the same job. A schedule flagged as needing review can be cleared with runwick schedules revalidate once you have fixed the cause. Every one of these actions is audited. IScheduleControl trusts the actor you pass; the HTTP API, dashboard and CLI check permissions. Next - Job context: read the occurrence in a handler. - Rate limits and concurrency

title: Installation
description: Install Runwick and one store package, add the optional packages you need, install the CLI and create the store's schema.
body: Runwick is split into small packages. Every app needs Runwick and exactly one store package. Everything else is optional. Packages Package Install when --- --- Runwick always, in any process that dispatches or runs jobs Runwick.Postgres your store is PostgreSQL Runwick.Sqlite your store is a SQLite file on one machine Runwick.Redis your store is a single Redis primary Runwick.Contracts you want to share job types with a project that has no database code. It holds IQueueJob , IJobHandler , the attributes and IJobDispatcher Runwick.AspNetCore you want the management HTTP API or the health checks Runwick.Dashboard you want the web dashboard. It brings in Runwick.AspNetCore Runwick.OpenTelemetry you want metrics and traces Runwick.Outbox you want the transactional outbox, plus Runwick.Outbox.Postgres or Runwick.Outbox.Sqlite for the source database Runwick.Testing reserved for test helpers. It has no public types in this release; see Testing for the patterns to use today Runwick.Cli a .NET tool, installed with dotnet tool install . The command is runwick Use the same version for every Runwick package. Add the packages Add the optional packages the same way, for example: The command line tool The runwick command migrates stores, raises one-time capabilities, and talks to the management API for jobs, queues and workers. See CLI for the full command list. Requirements - .NET 10. Every package targets net10.0 only. There are no .NET 8, .NET 9, .NET Framework or .NET Standard builds. - No Node or npm. The dashboard's web files ship inside its package. - One store: - PostgreSQL 16, 17 or 18 (18 is the reference version). Connect to the primary directly. - SQLite 3.38 or newer. The engine is bundled with Microsoft.Data.Sqlite , so there is nothing to install. The file must be on a local disk. - Redis 8.2 or newer, one standalone primary with durable settings (see below). The tested operating systems are Linux x64 and Windows x64. Runwick makes no claim for Native AOT or trimming. Create the schema Workers never change the schema when they start. You create it once, as a deployment step, before the first app starts. Running the migration again on a store that is already up to date does nothing. Each store has a MigrateAsync method, and the CLI runs the same code. Run the migration with a role that may create schemas. Everything goes into one schema, runwick , and that name cannot be changed. Your running app can then use a role with data access only. Use a file on a local disk. A file on a network share, or an in-memory database, is refused when the app starts. The server must run with these settings, or Runwick refuses to start: Replicas, Redis Cluster and Sentinel are refused. The CLI never takes a connection string as an argument. Pass the name of an environment variable with --connection-env , or pipe the string in with --connection-stdin . Next steps Define a job, register a worker and watch it run. Compare PostgreSQL, SQLite and Redis before you commit to one. Apply new migrations and raise capabilities when you move to a new version.

title: Outbox
description: Commit a job with your business data in a database that is not the job store, then let a relay deliver it at least once.
body: Staging only works when your business tables and Runwick's tables share one database. When they do not (your data is in one PostgreSQL database and the jobs in another, or the job store is Redis), no single transaction can span both. The outbox closes that gap: 1. Your transaction writes your rows and an outbox message to your own database. They commit together. 2. A relay reads committed messages and delivers each one to the Runwick store. 3. The store remembers each delivery, so a message the relay sends twice still creates one job, within a time window. Packages Package What it adds --- --- Runwick.Outbox The relay and the shared types ( OutboxStageOptions , OutboxRelayOptions , StagedOutboxMessage ) Runwick.Outbox.Postgres A PostgreSQL source: IPostgresOutbox , PostgresOutboxSchema , AddRunwickPostgresOutbox Runwick.Outbox.Sqlite A same-machine SQLite source: ISqliteOutbox , SqliteOutboxSchema , AddRunwickSqliteOutbox The source is your business database. The destination is the Runwick store the host is configured with: PostgreSQL, SQLite or Redis. Redis can be a destination but not a source. Set it up Run this once per source database, with a role that may create schemas. It creates a runwick outbox schema (PostgreSQL) or runwick outbox tables (SQLite) and returns the source's ID. It is safe to run again. For SQLite: await SqliteOutboxSchema.InstallAsync("Data Source=/var/lib/my-app/app.db"); (namespace Runwick.Outbox.Sqlite ). AddRunwickPostgresOutbox registers IPostgresOutbox and the relay, which runs as a hosted service. AddRunwickSqliteOutbox does the same for SQLite. Only one source adapter can be registered per host; a second registration throws. StageAsync writes inside a savepoint on your transaction. It never contacts the destination, and never commits, rolls back or retries your transaction. If it rejects the message, your transaction is left as it was. It returns a StagedOutboxMessage with the message ID, the proposed job ID and AcceptUntil , the end of the de-duplication window. Nothing is delivered until you commit. Staging options OutboxStageOptions Default Notes --- --- --- MessageId a new UUIDv7 A stable ID of your own. Staging the same ID with the same content again returns the stored message with Existing = true . The same ID with different content throws OutboxMessageConflictException . Never reuse an ID for something else. Dispatch none Ordinary DispatchOptions , frozen at staging time. AcceptanceHorizon 7 days How long the destination accepts and de-duplicates this message. Up to 30 days, whole milliseconds. Processes that only stage A process that stages but should not deliver can turn the relay off: relay: o = o.Enabled = false . It still needs AddRunwick with the destination store, because staging checks the destination. Before the runtime has connected to the store once, staging fails with outbox destination unknown . To stage before that, set the destination store's ID: destination: new OutboxDestination { StoreId = storeId } (the ID that the migration returned). Relay options OutboxRelayOptions Default Allowed --- --- --- Enabled true MaxInFlight 4 1 to 64 messages LeaseDuration 60 s at least 5 s, and at least 3 × RenewalInterval RenewalInterval 15 s positive ProviderCallTimeout 5 s positive, shorter than RenewalInterval IdlePoll 1 s positive. With a PostgreSQL source, the relay listens for new messages and polls every 5 s while the listener is healthy. RetryInitial / RetryMax 1 s / 60 s exponential, RetryMax at least RetryInitial TransportLifetime 30 s at most 30 s Bad values throw when you register the outbox. The relay opens at most two connections to the source. Several relays can serve one source: each message is leased to one relay at a time. The relay also deletes delivered rows from the source in small batches. The relay needs a destination store that accepts outbox deliveries; all three Runwick stores do. If the store does not, the relay fails when it starts. The de-duplication window Each message carries AcceptUntil : the time it was staged plus its acceptance horizon (7 days by default). Up to that moment, a message the relay delivers twice, after a lost reply or a crash, maps to the same job. The destination keeps that mapping until at least 24 hours after AcceptUntil . After AcceptUntil , the destination accepts nothing new for that message. If it was delivered in time, the relay finds the mapping and marks it delivered. If not, the message is blocked with horizon passed undelivered , so a person can decide. Restaging the same ID returns the original cutoff, never a longer one. To try again, stage a new message ID and accept that the work could happen twice. Blocked messages The relay blocks a message, rather than retrying it forever, when it cannot be delivered as written. Examples: the job type is no longer registered ( contract not registered ), the message was bound to another store or application ( destination binding mismatch ), the window passed ( horizon passed undelivered ), or the store rejected it. Blocked messages are never rewritten or retried automatically. They stay in the source table with state blocked and a blocked reason (in PostgreSQL, runwick outbox.outbox messages ). Fix the cause and reset the row to pending, or accept the loss. A destination that is simply down is not a reason to block: the relay retries with backoff. - Not exactly-once. Delivery is at-least-once with de-duplication inside the window. A delivered message means the store accepted it; the job itself is still at-least-once like any other. - No ordering. Messages are not delivered in the order they were staged, even from one source. - No de-duplication after the window , after the destination's mappings are cleaned up, or after the destination is restored from a backup without them. - No safe source restore beyond the destination's retained window. - SQLite sources are same-machine only. Every process that uses the SQLite file must run on one machine. Errors when staging Code Cause --- --- outbox message conflict The same message ID was staged with different content or destination. outbox destination unknown No OutboxDestination.StoreId , and the runtime has not connected to the store yet. outbox horizon invalid The horizon is not positive, exceeds 30 days, or is not whole milliseconds. outbox not installed The source schema is missing. Run InstallAsync . outbox schema incompatible The source schema has another version than this package. transaction invalid The transaction is completed, has no connection, or is read-only. None of these writes anything. A database error such as a deadlock or SQLITE BUSY reaches you unchanged; retry the whole transaction.

title: Testing
description: Test handlers as plain classes, fake IJobDispatcher in code that dispatches, and run end-to-end tests against a real SQLite file.
headings: End-to-end with a real SQLite file
When to test against PostgreSQL or Redis
body: Runwick's public surface is small and made of interfaces, so most tests need no special library: a handler is a plain class, and dispatching goes through IJobDispatcher . For the full path (dispatch, claim, run, finish), run a real worker against a temporary SQLite file. The Runwick.Testing package is reserved for test helpers (a recording dispatcher and a direct handler invoker), but in this release it does not contain any public types yet. The patterns on this page use only the main packages. Testing a handler A handler is a class with a HandleAsync method. Construct it with its dependencies and call it: Test the things Runwick relies on too: - Repeats are harmless. Call HandleAsync twice with the same job and check that the outside effect happened once, or that the same idempotency key was used both times. Runwick can and will run a handler more than once; see Delivery guarantees. - Cancellation is observed. Pass a cancelled token and check that the handler stops with an OperationCanceledException instead of finishing the work. - Permanent failures are permanent. If the handler throws PermanentJobFailureException for bad input, assert that it does. Handlers that use IJobContext IJobContext is an interface, so a test can pass its own implementation. A small fake with settable properties is enough: Then test, for example, that a handler uses the job ID as its idempotency key, or behaves differently on the last attempt: Testing code that dispatches IJobDispatcher has two methods. A recording fake that returns a receipt is a dozen lines: Use it in place of the real dispatcher: A fake cannot tell you whether the real store would accept the job: unknown queues, keys that are too long and payloads over 1 MiB are only refused by the real dispatcher. Cover those with an end-to-end test. To test how your code handles failures, make the fake throw the real exception types, for example DispatchOutcomeUnknownException or LocalCapacityExceededException . End-to-end with a real SQLite file SQLite needs no server, so a test can create a fresh database file, start a real host with a worker, dispatch a job and wait for the handler. The handler signals a TaskCompletionSource from dependency injection: Tips: - Give every test its own file. Runwick refuses in-memory databases, so a temporary file is the way to isolate tests. - Keep the temp directory on a local disk. A network share is refused. - Leave a generous timeout. Workers poll, and a fresh worker needs a moment to start. - Use the same registration code as production where you can, and swap only the store line. When to test against PostgreSQL or Redis All three stores give the same job behaviour, so SQLite covers most application tests. Test against your production store when the test depends on store-specific behaviour: staging jobs or completing them in your PostgreSQL transaction, connection limits, or Redis server settings. A disposable server per test run (for example with Testcontainers) works well. Remember to run the store's migration first.

title: Choosing a store
description: Compare PostgreSQL, SQLite and Redis as Runwick stores, see where each one stops, and pick a deployment shape.
body: All three stores give the same job behaviour: the same states, retries, receipts, uniqueness and rate rules. Your jobs and handlers do not change between them. The stores differ in where they can run, what they survive, and whether a job can share a transaction with your own data. At a glance PostgreSQL SQLite Redis --- --- --- --- Package Runwick.Postgres Runwick.Sqlite Runwick.Redis Server PostgreSQL 16, 17 or 18 (18 is the reference) a local file, SQLite 3.38 or newer (bundled) Redis 8.2 or newer, one standalone primary Hosts many, connected to the primary one machine only many, all reaching one primary Job or completion in the same transaction as your data yes, same database yes, same file no, use the outbox How workers notice new jobs LISTEN/NOTIFY wake-up, with polling as the fallback polling polling Refused at startup nothing listed; replicas and proxies are simply not certified a network share, an in-memory database, sync weaker than FULL a replica, Cluster, Sentinel, wrong persistence settings High availability not certified none none Runwick checks each store's durability settings when it starts and again while it runs. It refuses settings that could lose jobs rather than run on them. Which one to pick Pick PostgreSQL if you already run it, if your workers run on more than one host, or if you want to commit a job in the same transaction as your business data. It is the reference store: the one the rest of Runwick is measured against. Pick SQLite for a single-machine app, a desktop or edge service, or a small internal tool where running a database server is not worth it. Every process that uses the file must be on the same machine. Pick Redis if you already operate a durable Redis primary and do not need jobs to share a transaction with your business database. If you need that, put the outbox in your PostgreSQL or SQLite database and let it deliver to Redis. Limits to plan around PostgreSQL - Connect to the primary directly. Decisions about who owns a job never read from a replica. - High-availability setups and connection poolers (proxies) are not certified. If you use one, you are outside what has been tested. - The schema is always named runwick . You cannot change it. SQLite - One file on one machine. There is no multi-host support and no high availability. - Writes use WAL with synchronous=FULL . A weaker setting is refused. - Only one write happens at a time across all processes. Nothing here claims SQLite matches PostgreSQL's throughput. - Durability is whatever your disk and its fsync give you. Restoring the file from a backup is a break in history: receipts and uniqueness windows from before the restore do not carry over as one continuous record. - A test that kills a process is not a power-loss test, and Runwick does not claim it is. Redis - One primary, no high availability. Failover, Sentinel promotion and Cluster are not supported. A promoted replica may have lost jobs that were already acknowledged. - The server must run with appendonly yes , appendfsync always , no-appendfsync-on-rewrite no , maxmemory-policy noeviction and aof-load-truncated no . Redis without appendfsync always is not a supported configuration. - One application lives in one hash slot. Its throughput is bounded by one server thread, and one very large command can delay everything else for that application. - Redis cannot join your business transaction. There is no same-transaction completion. - Nothing here says Redis is faster than PostgreSQL. No speed comparison is claimed. Your jobs and handlers stay the same, so code written for one store runs on another by changing the Use... line. Jobs already in the old store stay there. Roles are configuration, not programs A Runwick process can take any combination of four roles: Role How you turn it on --- --- Producer any code that calls IJobDispatcher.DispatchAsync . Every app with AddRunwick can dispatch Worker runwick.AddWorker(...) Scheduler runwick.AddScheduler() Management app.MapRunwickManagement(...) , and optionally the dashboard There is nothing else to deploy. The store is the only shared piece, and processes never talk to each other directly. Deployment shapes Shape What runs where --- --- One app, embedded worker your web app dispatches and works in one process One app, external worker the web app only dispatches; a separate worker service runs the jobs Many replicas, embedded workers every replica both dispatches and works Replicas plus a worker tier the web tier only dispatches; a worker tier only works Mixed some replicas embed workers, and extra external workers run too PostgreSQL and Redis support all five shapes across hosts. SQLite supports all five as long as every process is on the same machine. A web app that only dispatches registers the store and the jobs, and leaves out AddWorker : The worker service registers the same jobs, plus handlers and a worker: Put the job records in a shared project that references only Runwick.Contracts , so the web app does not need your handler code. Worth knowing before you deploy - Automatic concurrency. AutoConcurrency(min, max) adjusts a pool inside one process. It does not coordinate across the cluster. - Schedules. Pausing a schedule stops new jobs from being created. It does not pause jobs the schedule already created. - The scheduler capability. Before any process can register a schedule, an operator raises the scheduler capability once per application with runwick store activate-capability --name scheduler . Until then, startup fails with scheduler not active . See Schedules. Next steps Connection strings, roles and the same-transaction APIs. File location, durability settings and single-machine limits. Required server settings and what Runwick checks while it runs. Migrations, shutdown timeouts and running workers in production.

title: Observability
description: Traces, metrics and logs from Runwick, how to export them with OpenTelemetry, and how to read the numbers.
body: Runwick uses the standard .NET tools and exports nothing unless you ask: - Traces: one ActivitySource named Runwick . - Metrics: one Meter named Runwick , with fixed names, units and attributes. - Logs: ILogger , with fixed event IDs. Payloads, credentials, connection strings and exception messages stay out by default. Job IDs may appear in spans and logs, never in metrics. Turning it on with OpenTelemetry Runwick.OpenTelemetry adds no exporter; use the one you already have. On the metrics side it keeps only Runwick's own attributes and sets a cardinality limit per instrument. Without OpenTelemetry, any listener works: subscribe to the Runwick source and meter by name (the constant is RunwickTelemetry.SourceName ). Options RunwickTelemetryOptions Default Meaning --- --- --- RecordExceptionDetails false Put a cleaned, size-limited exception message on spans and on log event 1011 MaxSeriesPerInstrument 1,000 Attribute combinations per instrument before measurements go to an overflow series (100 to 10,000) CollectApplicationMetrics false Make this process the application-wide collector ApplicationSamplePeriod 15 s How often the collector samples (5 s to 5 min) CollectorName "default" Value of the runwick.collector attribute If you raise MaxSeriesPerInstrument , pass the same number to AddRunwickInstrumentation(o = ...) so the SDK limit matches. Traces Span When --- --- send {queue} A dispatch, from prepare to confirmed reply stage {queue} Staging a job inside your own transaction process {queue} One attempt, from claim to stored result. Each attempt starts a new trace, linked to the dispatch runwick.begin , runwick.execute , runwick.attempt.cleanup , settle {queue} Steps inside process . Your handler's spans are children of runwick.execute runwick.recover Recovery of one expired lease runwick.schedule.materialize The scheduler creating jobs runwick.management.command A management change runwick.retention.batch One cleanup batch Lease renewals are not spans; they repeat too often. They show up in metrics. Metrics Durations are in seconds unless noted. Metric Type What it counts --- --- --- runwick.dispatch.operations Counter Dispatches by result, kind and queue runwick.dispatch.duration Histogram Dispatch time runwick.execution.authorized Counter Executions that started, by queue, job name and pool runwick.execution.duration Histogram Handler time, by queue, job name and outcome runwick.execution.start delay Histogram Time from due to start, by queue runwick.admission.deferred Counter Starts held back (for example by a rate limit), by reason runwick.attempt.cleanup.duration Histogram Time to dispose the job's DI scope runwick.settlement.duration Histogram Time to store a result, by settlement result runwick.storage.operation.duration Histogram Store calls, by operation, result and I/O class runwick.lease.renewals Counter Lease renewals by result runwick.lease.margin Histogram Lease time left at renewal, by pool runwick.lease.authority lost Counter Attempts that lost their lease, by reason runwick.recoveries Counter Expired leases recovered runwick.scaling.decisions Counter Automatic concurrency changes, by pool, direction and reason runwick.schedule.materialization.delay Histogram How late scheduled jobs were created runwick.schedule.occurrences Counter Schedule occurrences by disposition runwick.management.requests Counter Management requests by operation and result runwick.management.duration Histogram Management request time runwick.retention.rows Counter Rows deleted by cleanup, by record class runwick.retention.batches Counter Cleanup batches by class and result runwick.retention.batch.duration Histogram Cleanup batch time runwick.telemetry.dropped Counter Log records dropped by Runwick's own limits runwick.telemetry.overflow Counter Measurements sent to the overflow series runwick.worker.tickets Gauge Tickets by pool and phase runwick.worker.target Gauge Target ticket count by pool runwick.worker.oldest unsettled.age Gauge Oldest result not yet confirmed by the store, by pool runwick.worker.admission Gauge Whether a pool is claiming work runwick.retention.caught up.age Gauge Time since cleanup last caught up, by class runwick.queue.due Gauge, collector only Jobs waiting and due, by queue runwick.queue.oldest due.age Gauge, collector only Age of the oldest due job, by queue runwick.schedule.needs review Gauge, collector only Schedules that need review runwick.schedule.oldest overdue.age Gauge, collector only Most overdue schedule runwick.collector.snapshot.age Gauge, collector only Age of the collector's last sample In Prometheus the names become runwick queue due , runwick execution duration seconds bucket and so on. Logs Categories are Runwick.Worker , Runwick.Dispatch , Runwick.Scheduler , Runwick.Outbox , Runwick.Management , Runwick.Retention , Runwick.Store and Runwick.Telemetry . Every message has a fixed event ID, for example: ID Event --- --- 1003 A running attempt lost its lease 1004 A result could not be confirmed 1011 A handler failed 1101 A dispatch outcome is unknown 1202 A schedule needs review 1401 A management sign-in failed 1501 A cleanup batch failed 1701 A role cannot reach the store 1703 The store schema does not match this binary Warnings are limited to 10 a minute per event ID per process. The rest are counted and summarised once a minute (event 1603). Reading the numbers honestly - Local and application-wide numbers are different. Worker gauges describe one process and can be summed across processes. Queue depth and the oldest due job come only from processes with CollectApplicationMetrics = true . Usually that is one process, for example the standalone management host. - Never sum collector series. Runwick does not elect a collector. If two processes collect, both report the same queue. Use max by (runwick queue) ; the shipped dashboard and alerts do. - Missing is not zero. When a collector's sample is older than three periods, its queue gauges disappear instead of reporting 0, and runwick.collector.snapshot.age keeps growing. - "Due" is not "runnable". A due job may still wait for a concurrency slot, a rate limit, a paused queue or a worker that can run it. - A handler that succeeded is not a stored success. If the result could not be confirmed, the span says runwick.outcome = succeeded with runwick.settlement.result = unresolved . A replayed command is not counted twice. - Counts can be lost when a process crashes. Use them for operations, not for billing or audit. Grafana dashboard and Prometheus alerts Runwick.OpenTelemetry ships two files in its package content folder (they are also in the repository's ops folder): - content/grafana/runwick-overview.json : a Grafana dashboard with dispatch, execution, leases, pools, queues, schedules, management, retention and telemetry-health panels. - content/prometheus/runwick-alerts.yml : alert rules. Alert Fires when --- --- RunwickLeaseMarginLow The 5th percentile lease margin of a pool stays below 25 s RunwickAuthorityLost Any attempt lost its lease in the last 10 minutes RunwickSettlementOld A result has been unconfirmed for over 60 s RunwickDueAgeRising A queue's oldest due job has waited over 10 minutes RunwickFailuresRepeated More than 10% of a job type's executions do not succeed RunwickScheduleLag A schedule is over 2 minutes late or needs review RunwickRetentionFailing Cleanup fails repeatedly or has not caught up for 24 hours RunwickCollectorStale No fresh collector sample, or no collector at all RunwickStoreIncompatible Reads runwick host readiness incompatible , a gauge your host must export from its health checks. Runwick does not emit it The thresholds are not tuned for your workload. Adjust them, especially the due-age and failure-rate rules. The telemetry follows the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions version pinned in RunwickTelemetry.SemanticConventionsVersion , and no other.

title: Command line
description: The runwick CLI - contexts, job and queue controls, store administration, and stable output for scripts and agents.
body: runwick is a command-line tool with two halves: - Management commands ( jobs , queues , schedules , events , ...) talk to a management API over HTTPS, with your permissions, and are audited like any other caller. - Store commands ( migrate , store ... , and doctor with a connection) talk straight to the database, as the migration role. Install Self-contained single-file binaries also exist for Linux x64 and Windows x64. migrate applies the migrations built into the CLI. Use the CLI from the same Runwick release as your application. runwick doctor tells you when the CLI and the store disagree. Contexts and sign-in A context saves a server URL, a sign-in method, a user name and the name of an environment variable that holds the secret: - --url is the prefix you passed to MapRunwickManagement . It must be https:// , or http:// to a loopback address. - --auth basic sends a user and password; mutations fetch an antiforgery token automatically. - --auth bearer sends Authorization: Bearer . The server must map that API group with .ForMachineClients() . - Secrets are never written to the config file. The CLI looks for one in this order: --secret-stdin , the context's variable, RUNWICK SECRET , then a hidden prompt (only in human mode at a terminal). The config file is $RUNWICK CONFIG , or runwick/config.json in your application-data folder ( ~/.config/runwick/config.json on Linux). Use --context NAME or --url URL to override the current context for one command. Other commands: context list , context show , context remove . Jobs jobs list and jobs get never show payloads. Only the two reveal commands do, and the server writes an audit row for each. To create a job of a registered type from a JSON payload (needs Jobs.Dispatch ): --payload takes @file or - for standard input. A payload is never accepted inline. Queues, schedules and capacity Events, audit and settings Expected revisions Every change says which version of the target you were looking at. If someone else changed it in the meantime, you get stale revision (or stale generation ) and nothing happens. Two people acting on the same stale view cannot overwrite each other. In human and JSON mode you may leave out --expected-revision and --expected-generation . The CLI then reads the target first, uses what it read, and says which revision it used. In --agent mode they are required. Every change also has a command ID ( --command-id , generated when you leave it out). If the reply is lost, the CLI resends the same request with the same ID up to 3 times in 30 seconds. The server answers a resend with the original result, so nothing happens twice. If no answer arrives, the result is outcome unknown with the command ID; run the same command again with that --command-id . Store commands These run as the migration role. The connection string comes from an environment variable ( --connection-env ) or standard input ( --connection-stdin ). It is never accepted as an argument. Command What it does --- --- migrate Applies this CLI's migrations. Safe to run again store status Store ID and revision, the revision this CLI expects, each application's admission mode, and counts of leases and worker heartbeats store admission --mode ( open , drain , maintenance ) Drain stops new work and lets running work finish. Maintenance stops everything but status reads. Add --application for one application store activate-capability --name ( scheduler , rate admission ) Turns on a capability for an application. It cannot be undone store reidentify --confirm Gives a restored copy a new identity. Offline only --provider is postgres (default for store and doctor ), sqlite or redis . migrate requires it. How these fit together is in Upgrades. doctor Checks that the server is reachable, the credentials work, the API version matches and the clocks agree within 5 seconds. With a connection it also checks the store: its revision against the CLI's, and the store's durability settings. A check it could not run is reported as unverified , never as passed. Output for scripts and agents Flag Output --- --- (none) Tables and key: value lines for people. Errors go to stderr --output json The API's JSON body on stdout. Errors are JSON on stdout too, with a non-zero exit code --agent Exactly one JSON envelope per command on one line: ok , result , error (with code , retryable and hint ), commandId , the revisions it saw, and suggested nextActions runwick --agent describe prints every command with its arguments, options, required permission, error codes and exit codes. See AI agents for how to use it. Exit codes: Code Meaning --- --- 0 OK 1 Rejected (conflict, invalid state, not found) 2 Usage error 3 Outcome unknown; resend with the same command ID 4 Unavailable; retry 5 Not signed in or not allowed The CLI never prints secrets, cookies, tokens or connection strings, even with --verbose .

title: Troubleshooting
description: Common startup refusals, error codes and stuck jobs, each with its cause and the fix.
body: Runwick prefers refusing to start over running in a setup that could lose jobs. Most problems therefore show up as a clear error at startup, with a stable code. Every Runwick exception has a Code and a Disposition : KnownNotApplied means nothing was written, OutcomeUnknown means it may or may not have been. Startup refusals RunwickConfigurationException lists every problem at once, one per line, as [code] subject: message . Common codes: - invalid timing : worker timings break one of the startup rules, for example a shorter LeaseDuration without shorter renewals. See Startup validation. - invalid pool : a pool subscribes a queue that no job or Queue(...) call registers, subscribes one twice, or has a bad weight or size. - pool without queue , pool budget exceeded : a pool has no queue, or pool maximums add up to more than MaxOutstandingAttempts (16 by default). - missing store : no UsePostgres , UseSqlite or UseRedis , or an empty connection string. - invalid policy : a store option is out of range, or the SQLite connection string asks for something refused. Fix the listed settings. Runwick never adjusts a value for you. The application registers schedules, but the scheduler capability has not been raised. Start the application once so it registers, then, with the migration role: Use --provider sqlite or --provider redis for those stores, and --name rate admission if you use rate limits. Restart afterwards. This is done once per application and cannot be undone. See Schedules. The store has not been migrated, or it was migrated by a different Runwick version than the one running. Workers never migrate on startup. Run the migration with the same Runwick version as the app: or RunwickPostgresMigrations.MigrateAsync / RunwickSqliteMigrations.MigrateAsync / RunwickRedisMigrations.MigrateAsync from code. See Upgrades for the order of steps when the version changes. The application was drained or put in maintenance (for example during an upgrade), so new processes are refused with AdmissionClosedException ( admission closed ). Reopen it when the upgrade is done: Then start the process again. The error is safe to retry. - server version unsupported : PostgreSQL 16 or later is required. - encoding unsupported : the database must use UTF8 . Create a new database with that encoding. - migration lock unavailable : another migration runner held the lock for 60 seconds. Wait for it to finish, or find the stuck session. Run migrations with a role that may create the runwick schema. The app's own role does not need that right. SQLite The file is on a UNC path or network drive (Windows) or on a network filesystem such as NFS, SMB/CIFS, 9p or sshfs (Linux). The message names the filesystem type. SQLite's locking is not safe across machines, so Runwick refuses it. Move the file to a local disk. If several machines must share jobs, use PostgreSQL or Redis. A connection did not end up in WAL mode with synchronous = FULL and foreign keys = ON . The usual cause is a file that was never migrated: the migration switches the file to WAL. Run RunwickSqliteMigrations.MigrateAsync (or runwick migrate --provider sqlite ) on the same file. In-memory databases ( :memory: , Mode=Memory ), an empty Data Source , Mode=ReadOnly , Cache=Shared and Foreign Keys=False are refused. Point Data Source at a file. In tests, use a temporary file per test; see Testing. Your transaction started deferred and could not take the write lock when it first wrote. Runwick passes the error through unchanged. Begin transactions that stage jobs with BeginTransaction(deferred: false) , keep them short, and retry the whole transaction. Redis The store's check found a setting it cannot run on. The error names the setting and the value it saw, for example appendfsync=everysec or maxmemory-policy=allkeys-lru . Set these on the server and restart the app: A value reported as unverifiable means an ACL blocked CONFIG GET or MODULE LIST . Allow both for Runwick's user. Managed services that hide CONFIG are not supported. See Redis. Runwick needs exactly one standalone primary. It refuses a configuration string with several endpoints or a Sentinel service name, and a server that reports itself as a replica or as part of a Cluster. Point the app at the primary only. A recheck (every 30 seconds by default) found a changed setting, for example someone ran CONFIG SET appendfsync everysec . Runwick stops sending new work until a later check passes; calls already sent finish. Restore the settings. Work resumes on its own. Redis came back empty (for example after FLUSHALL ), with another store's identity, or with an older revision than this process saw (for example a restored backup or a promoted replica). Runwick stops admitting work and treats every lease it held as lost. Check what happened to the server. Restart the processes only once the store's history is the one you want to keep, and accept that recent work may be lost or repeated. Dispatching The request was sent, but no answer came back: a timeout, a dropped connection, or your cancellation token fired after sending. The job may or may not exist. Do not dispatch a new job blindly. Use the operation ID and the prepared request on the exception: See Delivery guarantees. Too many dispatch calls were waiting in this process: more than 64 waiting for one of 8 slots, or a wait longer than 1 second. Nothing was sent. Retry with backoff, dispatch in batches with DispatchManyAsync , or raise ProducerOptions.MaxConcurrentCalls (this adds database connections on PostgreSQL). A prepared dispatch was sent after its deadline (5 minutes after it was prepared, by default). It can never apply. Prepare a new one. The same operation ID was sent with different content. A prepared dispatch must be re-sent unchanged. For management commands and the CLI, use a new --command-id for a different request. A window key was reused with a different payload or options, or a window key and an active key point at two different jobs. Runwick refuses rather than hand back an unrelated job. UniquenessConflictException.ConflictingJobId names the existing job. Check how you build the key. See Uniqueness. StageAsync or CompleteInTransactionAsync refused your transaction: it is completed, read-only or has no connection; it points at a different database or file from the store; or (SQLite) its connection lacks foreign keys = 1 and synchronous = FULL . See Transactions. Running jobs The handler called CompleteInTransactionAsync but returned while the transaction was still open, or after rolling it back. Commit before the handler returns. If you roll back on purpose and want a retry, throw an exception instead of returning. The worker no longer owns the job, usually because its lease expired during a long pause or a long transaction. Roll back your transaction. Another worker may run the job. Keep transactions inside handlers short, and check that the process is not starved of CPU. That is allowed: delivery is at-least-once. It happens after a crash, a lost lease or a lost reply. Make the handler safe to repeat with an idempotency key, or use transactional completion for changes in the same database. See Delivery guarantees. Check, in this order: - a worker pool subscribes the job's queue ( p.Queues(...) ), and a worker process is running; - the queue is not paused ( runwick queues list ); - the job has no NotBefore in the future; - a rate limit or concurrency limit is not holding it back; - the application is not drained ( runwick store status ). The dashboard shows queue state, workers and why work is waiting. Runwick's shutdown takes up to 25 seconds: 15 to drain, 5 to cancel, 5 to finish. If the host's own shutdown timeout is shorter, the host stops first. Keep HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout (30 s by default) above WorkerOptions.ShutdownBudget , and make handlers observe their CancellationToken . The relay found a message it cannot deliver as written: the job type is no longer registered ( contract not registered ), the window passed ( horizon passed undelivered ), or the store rejected it. Blocked messages are never retried automatically. Read blocked reason in the outbox table, fix the cause and reset the row to pending, or accept the loss. See Outbox. Management API and CLI Every change takes the revision you last saw, so two operators cannot overwrite each other. Someone (or the job itself) changed the target since you read it. The response includes the current revision. Read the target again, check it is still the change you want, and retry with the new revision (and generation, for jobs). The target's state does not allow the action (for example retrying a job that is still running), or it is already in that state. Read it again. Agent mode never prompts. Give the secret through the context's secret variable, RUNWICK SECRET or --secret-stdin . Mutations in agent mode need --expected-revision (and --expected-generation for jobs); the error's next action tells you which read to run first. See AI agents.

title: Retries and timeouts
description: How many times a job runs, how long Runwick waits between tries, how execution timeouts work, and how failures are recorded.
headings: Retrying a failed job by hand
body: When a handler fails, Runwick waits a little and runs it again, up to a budget. When the budget is spent, the job ends in failed and stays there until someone retries it. Setting Default Where --- --- --- MaxExecutions 3 (the first run plus up to two retries) attribute, fluent, JobDefaults Retry delay 5 s first, doubling, never more than 60 s, half-random fluent, JobDefaults ExecutionTimeout none fluent, JobDefaults These values are copied onto the job when it is dispatched. Changing the configuration later does not change jobs already in the queue. MaxExecutions MaxExecutions counts runs that actually started : each time a worker is authorized to call your handler. It includes the first run, so MaxExecutions(3) means at most two automatic retries. The allowed range is 1 to 100. Precedence, later wins: library default, then JobDefaults , then the attribute, then fluent job configuration. Crashes before the handler starts A worker can claim a job and die before calling the handler, for example during a deploy. No user code ran, so Runwick does not charge MaxExecutions for it. It counts these on a separate guard instead: after 5 consecutive claims that never started, the job fails with reservation abandonment exhausted . The delay between these re-queues starts at 1 second and grows to 30 seconds. A crash in the tiny window right after a run is authorized but before your method is called still costs one execution. Retry delay After a failed run, the next try waits an exponential delay with "equal jitter": the nominal delay is initial × 2^(n−1) , capped at the maximum, and the actual delay is a random value between half the nominal and the full nominal. The randomness spreads out jobs that failed together. With the defaults (5 s initial, 60 s maximum): After run Waits between --- --- 1 2.5 s and 5 s 2 5 s and 10 s 3 10 s and 20 s 5 and later 30 s and 60 s Both values must be whole milliseconds, from 1 ms to 24 hours, and the initial delay must not exceed the maximum. There is no attribute for the retry delay. The chosen delay is stored with the outcome. If the store's reply is lost and the write is repeated, the same delay is reused. What counts as a failure What the handler does Outcome --- --- Returns normally Succeeded Throws any exception Retryable failure Throws PermanentJobFailureException Permanent failure: no more retries Runs past ExecutionTimeout Timed out (retryable) Stops because of a user cancel Cancelled Stops because the worker is shutting down Interrupted (retryable) Payload cannot be decoded or upgraded Permanent failure A retryable outcome is retried only while the budget lasts. After that the job is failed . Failing permanently Throw PermanentJobFailureException when retrying cannot help, such as invalid input: The code follows the name grammar ( A-Z a-z 0-9 . - , up to 128 characters). Deciding in middleware Middleware can turn exceptions into explicit results: Retry(reason, delay) still uses up one execution. The delay is used as given (no jitter), capped at the job's maximum retry delay. A null delay uses the normal policy. A negative delay is a contract fault and fails the job permanently. Execution timeout There is no timeout by default. Set one per job or for the whole application: The timeout must be a whole number of milliseconds, at most 30 days. There is no attribute for it. When the time is up, Runwick: 1. records the cause Timeout and cancels the handler's CancellationToken ; 2. waits up to the cancellation grace (10 seconds) for the handler to return; 3. records the run as timed out , even if the handler then returned normally. A timed-out run is retryable and costs one execution. The clock measures the local pipeline: from the moment the worker starts the run, including decoding, DI and middleware, until the handler's task completes. It does not measure what happened in the outside world. A payment that went through just before the timeout fired still went through. .NET cannot safely stop running code. If the handler ignores the token, it keeps running after the grace period. The worker then stops renewing the lease and writes no result; the job is recovered after the lease expires and may run again elsewhere. See Cancellation. How failures are recorded Every run is an attempt , and every attempt is kept (until retention removes it) with: - its outcome (succeeded, retryable failure, permanent failure, timed out, interrupted, cancelled, abandoned); - an error code, the exception type and message; - the full exception text, capped at 16 KiB with a truncation marker. A Failed(code, message) message longer than 1,024 bytes is truncated. Exception text can contain sensitive data. The dashboard, API and CLI show it only with a separate permission, and each reveal is audited: Retrying a failed job by hand A failed or cancelled job can be retried from the dashboard, the API or the CLI. This starts a new generation of the same job ID with a fresh execution budget. The old attempts stay in the history. In C , use IJobControl.RetryAsync from Runwick.Management . See Management API. Next - Cancellation: how the token works. - Delivery guarantees: why a run can repeat.

title: Dashboard
description: A web UI for jobs, queues, workers and schedules, served from inside your ASP.NET Core app.
headings: Order with your own Inertia app
body: Runwick.Dashboard is a web UI that runs inside your own ASP.NET Core app. It reads and acts through the same layer as the management API, so it has the same permissions, limits and audit trail. Its web files are embedded in the package; you do not need Node or npm. !Job details Setting it up The dashboard needs AddRunwickManagement , because it uses its sign-in schemes and grant mapping by default. AddRunwickDashboard takes a mount ID (1 to 32 characters of a-z , 0-9 and - ). You can register several mounts with different IDs and map each at its own path. MapRunwickDashboard(path, mountId) uses "default" when you leave out the ID. You do not have to call MapRunwickManagement for the dashboard to work. Map it only if you also want the JSON API or the CLI. Options DashboardOptions Default Meaning --- --- --- Title "Runwick" Page title SignOutPath null Your own sign-out route, as a path on the same site, including any path base. The button posts an empty form to it. null hides the button AuthenticationSchemes(...) The management schemes Schemes this mount accepts MapGrants(...) The management grant map Grants on this mount Actor(...) The management actor map The actor written to audit Per-mount schemes are useful when the JSON API uses bearer tokens for machine clients and the dashboard uses cookies for people. Order with your own Inertia app The dashboard is built on Inertia.Net. If your app also uses Inertia, map the dashboard before your own UseInertia() : Otherwise your app's Inertia middleware version-checks the dashboard's requests and sends its pages into a reload loop. Runwick cannot detect the wrong order, so this is on you. The dashboard owns everything under its path. If one of your endpoints has a route under it, Runwick logs a critical error and stops the application once it has started. Until that check has run, the dashboard answers 503 . Permissions Each page needs the permission behind the data it shows, and each button needs the permission for its action. The navigation lists only the pages the caller may open; other pages answer 403 . Page Needs --- --- Overview, Jobs, Runs, Run Jobs.Read Queues, Queue Queues.Read (pause and resume: Queues.Control ) Workers, Pools, Scaling Capacity.Read (set capacity: Capacity.Edit ) Schedules, Schedule Schedules.Read Settings Settings.Read Retention Settings.Read (edit: Retention.Manage ) Audit Audit.Read A payload or an error detail is hidden until someone with Jobs.ReadPayload or Jobs.ReadError clicks reveal, and every reveal writes an audit row. Errors show only their code until revealed. Hiding a button is a convenience, not security: the server checks every request again. What you see - Overview: key figures with small trend lines, recent failures, queues and recent scaling events. - Jobs and Runs: each job type with its numbers, then the individual runs with filters by queue, state, name and time range. Cancel, retry and rerun from the list or the run page. - Run: a job's status history, its attempts and the resources each attempt used. - Queues, Workers, Pools, Schedules: each with a detail page. Pause and resume queues and schedules, trigger a schedule, set a concurrency limit. - Retention and Audit: the cleanup policy with its progress, and the trail of who did what. Lists show 50 rows a page with a "Next" link. There are no page counts or grand totals. Each list says when it was read ("as of 12:04:31"). What it is not - Not live. Pages poll every few seconds while the tab is visible (5 s at the fastest, and you can pick a slower interval or turn it off). There is no push channel. - No queue-depth totals of its own. Figures on the Overview are tallies of what one read returned, shown as "50+" when there is more. - "Cancel requested" is not "stopped". Cancellation is cooperative; a running handler stops only when it honours its token. See Cancellation. - A revealed payload cannot be taken back from a browser that has seen it. - Permissions are per application and queue, not per tenant. - Rate limits are per process. Several replicas each allow the full rate. Running it on its own The dashboard does not need a worker in the same process. A small internal app with only AddRunwick , AddRunwickManagement and AddRunwickDashboard is a common shape. See A standalone management host. The repository's samples/Runwick.Dashboard.Host shows a complete host: cookie sign-in, three users with different grants, a path base, and the dashboard mounted before the host's own Inertia pages.

title: Uniqueness
description: Stop duplicate jobs from being created with active keys and window keys, and know what uniqueness does not prevent.
body: Uniqueness stops the same job from being created twice . A user double-clicks "Sign up", or a client retries a request whose response was lost: you want one job, not two. Runwick has two kinds of key, for two different questions: Key Question Held for --- --- --- Active key "Is one of these already queued or running?" As long as the job is pending , reserved , running or retrying Window key "Did I already ask for exactly this?" A fixed time after the first dispatch, even after the job finished Keys are scoped to the application and the job name. The same key on two different job types does not collide. Active keys While a job with a given active key is waiting or running, another dispatch with the same key creates nothing. It returns the existing job with Disposition = Reused and DuplicateMatch = Active . When the job finishes (succeeded, failed or cancelled) the key is free again. Use it for work where a second copy in the queue is pointless, such as "recalculate statistics for tenant X". The second dispatch's payload is discarded. Check receipt.Disposition if you need to know that your payload was not the one stored. Window keys A window key makes a dispatch idempotent for a fixed time. For the length of the window after the first dispatch, any dispatch with the same key and the same request returns the same job, even if that job finished hours ago. The window does not slide. It is measured from the first dispatch, so retrying with the same key cannot keep it alive forever. After the window the key is forgotten and a new dispatch creates a new job. There is no default window; you always choose it. It must be positive, in whole milliseconds, and at most 3,650 days. Same key, different request Runwick stores a fingerprint of what you asked for: the payload, job name, queue, priority, start time, keys, resource keys and business metadata. If you reuse a window key with a different request, that is not a retry. It is a bug or a key collision, and dispatch fails with UniquenessConflictException ( uniqueness conflict ) instead of quietly handing back an unrelated job. The exception's ConflictingJobId names the existing job. A difference only in retry or timeout settings (for example after you changed a default) is not a conflict. The dispatch returns the existing job with PolicyDrift = true , and the existing job keeps its original settings. Using both A dispatch can carry both keys: The window key makes retries of this request safe. The active key makes any request for that user collapse onto one queued job. If a new window key meets an existing active job, the window key is linked to that job, so later retries find it even after it finishes. If the two keys point at two different jobs, dispatch fails with uniqueness composition conflict . Declared keys are required When a job type declares UniqueWhileActive or UniqueWithinWindow , that key is required for every dispatch of it. There is no option to skip it. - If the dispatch also passes an explicit key for the same dimension, the two must be equal (and the windows equal), or it fails with uniqueness key mismatch . - A selector that returns null fails with uniqueness required . A selector that throws fails with key selector failed . - Selectors run once, when the dispatch is prepared. Keep them pure and fast. Job types without declared keys can pass keys per dispatch, or not. Key rules - 1 to 512 bytes as UTF-8. - Valid Unicode with no control characters. - Case-sensitive and compared exactly: no trimming, no case folding, no Unicode normalization. A key that breaks these rules fails with invalid key before anything is written. In batches In DispatchManyAsync , items behave as if dispatched one after another in input order. A later item that matches an earlier one is Reused . Conflicts fail the whole batch unless you set ContinueOnConflict . See Dispatching. What uniqueness does not do Uniqueness is about inserting jobs. It is not an execution lock and it never promises a handler runs once. You want to avoid… Use --- --- Two copies queued at once Active key A client retry creating a second job Window key Two jobs touching the same thing at the same moment A resource scope with capacity 1 A repeated run having a visible effect twice Idempotent handlers: pass an idempotency key to the other side (see Delivery guarantees) Things to keep in mind: - An active key is about being queued. Retries and crash recovery can still run the job more than once. - A window key lives in the store. Restoring the database from a backup can bring back or lose keys. - Window keys are not tied to job retention. A key can outlive the job's history, and the reused job may already be cleaned up. Next - Rate limits and concurrency - Delivery guarantees

title: Introduction
description: Runwick is a background-job library for .NET 10 that stores jobs in PostgreSQL, SQLite or Redis and runs them on workers you control.
headings: What it promises, and what it does not
body: Runwick is a background-job library for .NET 10. Your app writes a job to a store (PostgreSQL, SQLite or Redis), and a worker picks it up and runs your handler. The worker can run inside your app or in a separate process. It is a library, not a service. There is no Runwick server to deploy. The store is the single source of truth, and workers never talk to each other: they talk to the store. !Runwick dashboard: a job's details, status history and the resources each attempt used How it works A job is a plain record with a stable name. A handler is a class that knows what to do with it. DispatchAsync returns only after the store has confirmed the write. A worker reserves the job from the store, holds a lease on it while it runs, and records the result. If the handler fails and there are attempts left, the job waits for a retry delay and runs again. If it runs out of attempts, it ends up failed , where an operator can retry it. Producer, worker, scheduler and management are roles, not separate programs. One process can take any combination of them. See Choosing a store for the common shapes. What you get - Three stores, one API. PostgreSQL is the reference store, for many hosts. SQLite suits a single machine. Redis needs one durable primary. Your jobs and handlers do not change between them. - Retries and timeouts. Each job has an execution budget (3 by default) and an exponential, partly random retry delay. Timeouts are off unless you set one. - Queues and priorities. Worker pools read named queues with high, medium and low lanes. Queues can be paused. - Uniqueness, rate limits and concurrency caps. All off until you declare them. - Schedules. Cron and one-time schedules that create at most one job per occurrence. - Same-transaction work. On PostgreSQL and SQLite, you can create a job, or complete one, in the same transaction as your own data. - Transactional outbox. Commit a message with your business data, then deliver it to any store. - Operations. A management HTTP API, a web dashboard and the runwick command line. All three share the same permissions and audit trail. - Observability. OpenTelemetry traces and metrics, structured logs and health checks. What it promises, and what it does not Runwick's guarantees are deliberately narrow, and the docs say so plainly. - At-least-once delivery. A handler can run more than once: after a crash, a lost lease or a lost reply. Write handlers that are safe to repeat, and pass an idempotency key to outside systems. - One exactly-once case. If your handler's effect is a change in the same PostgreSQL or SQLite database as Runwick's tables, the change and the job's completion can commit together. Nothing else is exactly-once: not emails, not HTTP calls, not Redis. - Cooperative cancellation. Cancelling a job signals its CancellationToken . Runwick cannot stop code that ignores the token. - A lease running out does not prove the old handler stopped. Two copies of a handler can briefly overlap. - Durable settings are checked, not assumed. Runwick refuses store settings that could lose jobs, such as SQLite without synchronous=FULL or Redis without appendfsync always . The API and storage formats can still change before 1.0. The work to certify the stores for 1.0 (Windows and macOS checks, a reference benchmark and a 24-hour soak test) is not finished, so no store is labelled "certified" yet. Delivery guarantees has the full list. Requirements - .NET 10. Every package targets net10.0 only. - One store: PostgreSQL 16, 17 or 18; a local SQLite file (the engine is bundled); or Redis 8.2 or newer. - No Node or npm. The dashboard's web files are inside its package. Next steps Pick the packages for your store, install the CLI and create the schema. Go from an empty project to a job that runs, in five steps. PostgreSQL, SQLite or Redis: what each supports and where each stops. What at-least-once means for your handlers, and the one exactly-once case. Job names, attributes, dependency injection and the job context. See queues, jobs and workers, and retry or cancel jobs from the browser.

title: Transactions
description: Create a job, or mark one as succeeded, inside your own PostgreSQL or SQLite transaction so it commits with your data or not at all.
headings: Completing a job in your transaction
body: When your business tables and Runwick's tables live in the same PostgreSQL database or the same SQLite file, one transaction can hold both. Runwick uses that in two places: - Staging a job. Create a job in the same transaction as your own rows. Either both are saved, or neither is. - Completing a job. A handler marks its job as succeeded in the same transaction as the changes it made. This is Runwick's one exactly-once case. Redis cannot join a business transaction. With Redis, or with a business database that is not the job store, use the outbox. PostgreSQL SQLite --- --- --- Stage a job IPostgresJobDispatcher.StageAsync ISqliteJobDispatcher.StageAsync Stage a batch StageManyAsync (up to 100 jobs) StageManyAsync (up to 100 jobs) Complete the current job IPostgresJobCompletion.CompleteInTransactionAsync ISqliteJobCompletion.CompleteInTransactionAsync Transaction type NpgsqlTransaction SqliteTransaction Namespace Runwick.Postgres Runwick.Sqlite All of these are registered by UsePostgres or UseSqlite . You do not add anything else. Staging a job StageAsync takes the same DispatchOptions as DispatchAsync (queue, priority, NotBefore , uniqueness, metadata). It returns a StagedDispatch with the job ID and whether the job was Created or Reused by a uniqueness key. It is not a DispatchReceipt , because nothing is durable until you commit. Rules: - Runwick never commits, rolls back, disposes or retries your transaction. - A serialization failure or deadlock (PostgreSQL), or SQLITE BUSY (SQLite), reaches you unchanged. Retry the whole transaction. To reuse the same operation on a retry, prepare once with IPreparedJobDispatcher.Prepare and pass the PreparedDispatch to StageAsync each time. - On PostgreSQL, a committed staged job wakes idle workers through the same notification as a normal dispatch. A rolled-back one never does. Checks on your transaction Before writing anything, Runwick checks the transaction. A failure throws TransactionValidationException and leaves your transaction as it was. Code Cause --- --- transaction invalid The transaction is completed, has no connection, or is read-only. transaction store mismatch The connection points at a different database or file from the configured store. transaction profile mismatch SQLite only: the connection does not have foreign keys = 1 and synchronous = FULL . Completing a job in your transaction Inject IPostgresJobCompletion (or ISqliteJobCompletion ) into the handler. It only works inside a running attempt. If the process crashes before the commit, the credit and the "succeeded" mark both vanish, and the job runs again. If it crashes after the commit, both are saved and the job never runs again. Either way, the credit is applied exactly once. Rules for completion A second call in the same attempt throws JobCompletionException with completion already staged . A call outside an attempt, or after the handler has returned, throws no active attempt . If the worker no longer owns the job (its lease expired and another worker may have it), CompleteInTransactionAsync throws JobOwnershipLostException . Roll back your transaction. Your changes must not commit without the completion. When the handler returns, Runwick looks for the staged completion. If your transaction is still open, or was rolled back while the handler returned normally, the job fails permanently with staged completion not committed . If you rolled back on purpose and want a retry, throw an exception instead of returning. While your transaction holds the staged completion, it also holds a lock on the job's row, so lease renewal for that job pauses. A transaction that stays open too long can outlive the lease (60 seconds by default). On SQLite, every Runwick write on the file waits while your write transaction is open. If the commit succeeds and something throws afterwards, the job still counts as succeeded; the exception is kept for diagnostics only. If the reply to your COMMIT is lost but the commit went through, Runwick finds the stored outcome and never runs the handler again. What this does not cover Transactional completion covers changes in that one database or file. It does not cover emails, HTTP calls, message brokers, other databases or Redis. A handler that sends an email and then completes in a transaction can still send the email twice. For those, use idempotency keys; see Delivery guarantees. - It does not make the handler run once. A handler can still start more than once; only the committed effects are applied once. - Staging is not available on Redis. - A restored database is a break in history. Completions and receipts from before the restore are not guaranteed to behave as one continuous record. For effects outside the database, a common pattern combines both tools: record "already done" in your own table in the same transaction as the completion, and pass an idempotency key to the outside service. If the process crashes between sending and committing, the next run sends again with the same key, and a provider that honours idempotency keys ignores the duplicate.

title: Rate limits and concurrency
description: Cap how many jobs run at once and how many start per time window, per process or across every worker.
headings: Per process or across all workers
body: There are two different limits, and they answer different questions: Concurrency limit Rate limit --- --- --- Question How many run at the same time ? How many start per window of time? Example "At most 5 PDF renders at once" "At most 100 calls to the email API per minute" Checked when a worker claims the job the run is authorized, just before the handler A 1 ms job barely touches a concurrency limit but counts fully against a rate limit. A 10-minute job holds a concurrency slot the whole time but counts once against a rate limit. Per process or across all workers Some limits live in one process's memory. Others live in the store and hold across every worker. Setting Scope --- --- FixedConcurrency(n) / AutoConcurrency(min, max) on a pool This process, this pool MaxOutstandingAttempts(n) on a worker (default 16) This process, all pools runwick.Queue("q", q = q.MaxConcurrent(n)) All workers MaxConcurrent(n) on a job All workers PerResource(selector, n) on a job All workers, per key RollingWindow(...) , RollingWindowPerResource(...) All workers Four processes with FixedConcurrency(8) run up to 32 jobs. If you need "5 at most, anywhere", use a store-backed limit. Pool sizing is covered in Workers. Concurrency caps A store-backed concurrency limit is called a scope . Each scope has a capacity. A job that needs a scope must get a free slot in it when it is claimed; a crashed worker's slot frees itself when its lease runs out. Kind Key Example --- --- --- queue the queue name emails , capacity 20 job-type the job name pdf.render , capacity 5 resource what your selector returns invoice:123 , capacity 1 A job can need several scopes at once, for example its queue, its type and two resources. It must get a slot in all of them or it waits. The limit is 8 scopes per job ( too many scopes ). All capacities must be at least 1. A resource scope with capacity 1 is a distributed lock on one thing. Use it for "never recalculate the same account twice at the same time". Uniqueness cannot do this: it controls creating jobs, not running them. The resource selector The selector runs once, when the job is dispatched. Its result is stored with the job. Keep it a pure function of the payload. The key follows the same rules as uniqueness keys: 1 to 512 UTF-8 bytes, no control characters, case-sensitive. A throwing selector fails the dispatch with key selector failed . Changing a capacity Queue and job-type scopes are created at startup if they do not exist. Resource scopes are created by the first dispatch that needs them. An existing scope is never overwritten from code. If you change MaxConcurrent(5) to MaxConcurrent(10) and redeploy, the stored capacity stays 5 and the difference is reported as drift. Change a live capacity with the CLI, the dashboard or ICapacityControl : Lowering a capacity revokes nothing. Jobs already running keep their slots; new claims wait until the count drops below the new limit. Fencing tokens A worker can lose its lease and keep running, for example after a long pause. With a capacity-1 resource scope, another worker can then take the slot while the first one is still writing. Runwick cannot stop the first worker's code, but each new holder of a capacity-1 resource scope gets a fencing token : a number that only goes up. The token only protects you if the other system remembers the highest value it has seen and rejects lower ones. Rate limits A rate limit allows at most N run authorizations in any rolling window of time: Bound Value --- --- Limit 1 to 100,000 per window Window whole milliseconds, 1 second to 24 hours Rate scopes per job at most 8, and at most one RollingWindow for the job type "Rolling" means the window always ends now. It is never "this calendar minute", so 200 cannot slip through across a minute boundary. What happens at the limit When a scope is full, the job is deferred : it goes back to waiting with a new earliest start time, roughly when the oldest run in the window drops out (at least 250 ms later, plus up to 100 ms of jitter). A deferral costs nothing: no execution, no retry budget. The worker's slot is freed at once. The deferral time is a hint, not a reservation; another worker may take the capacity first. If a job needs several rate scopes, it needs room in all of them, or none is charged. A run that fails after it was authorized keeps its charge, and its retry needs a new one. What a rate limit counts The limit counts authorizations, the moment Runwick says "run now". It does not count your handler's later HTTP calls. A handler that waits five minutes before calling the API, or calls it three times, is not tracked. If your provider is strict, add a limiter around the HTTP client too. Turn on rate admission first Rate limits need the store capability rate admission , raised once per application. Until then, dispatching a job that has a rate limit is refused with rate admission not active and nothing is written. This registers the application in the store. Use --provider sqlite or --provider redis for the other stores. From code: RunwickPostgresMigrations.ActivateCapabilityAsync(connectionString, "my-app", "rate admission", "deploy") (the SQLite and Redis migration classes have the same method). The step is done once per application. A capability is never lowered. After activation, older Runwick binaries that do not know rate admission can no longer create jobs for that application. Upgrade every process first. See Upgrades. Rate scopes, like concurrency scopes, are created by the first dispatch that needs them and are not overwritten from code later. Next - Workers: pool sizes and automatic concurrency. - Queues and priorities

title: Health checks
description: Liveness and per-role readiness checks for ASP.NET Core, and how to map them for your orchestrator.
body: Runwick.AspNetCore plugs Runwick's health into the standard ASP.NET Core health checks. No extra package is needed beyond that. Adding the checks Call AddRunwick() on the health-check builder after AddRunwick (and after AddRunwickManagement , if you use it). It looks at what the host has registered and adds: Check Tag Added when --- --- --- runwick-live live Always runwick-producer ready Always runwick-worker ready The host calls AddWorker runwick-scheduler ready The host calls AddScheduler runwick-management ready The host calls AddRunwickManagement Mapping the endpoints Use the tags to split liveness from readiness: Then point your orchestrator at them. For Kubernetes: What each check means Check Healthy Degraded Unhealthy --- --- --- --- Live The worker's internal timer keeps ticking The timer stalled. A store outage alone never makes liveness fail Producer The startup compatibility check passed and the last store call worked The last call failed less than 30 s ago Incompatible schema, or failing for 30 s or more Worker Claiming and finishing work normally Partly impaired Draining, store outage, every pool stopped under pressure, or incompatible store Scheduler Compatible and recently wrote its progress A recent write failed Incompatible, or writes keep failing Management Configuration valid and the periodic store read works A read failed less than 30 s ago Failing for 30 s or more A few details worth knowing: - Checks never wait on the store. They return cached state. Background refreshers update it every 10 seconds with a 1 second budget. A health request never claims a job. - Stale is not healthy. If a refresher has not succeeded for three periods, the check reports Degraded with reason stale . - Draining makes a worker not ready, but still alive. That is what you want during an upgrade: the orchestrator stops sending traffic but does not restart the process. - An empty queue, a paused queue or a backlog nobody can run does not change readiness. Readiness is about whether this process can do its job, not about the work. Reasons stay private by default Each result carries a short reason code ( ok , stale , store unavailable , incompatible , ...) in its description. The default response writer prints only the overall status, so public endpoints show Healthy , Degraded or Unhealthy and nothing more. If you want the reasons, write a detailed response and put it behind your own authorization: Without ASP.NET Core The same data is available from IRunwickHealth in dependency injection: Liveness() returns one RunwickRoleHealth , Readiness() returns one per enabled role, each with Role , Status , Reason and ObservedAt . A worker service without a web server can expose it however your platform expects, for example by touching a file. The shipped Prometheus rule RunwickStoreIncompatible reads a gauge that your host exports, set to 1 while any runwick- readiness check reports reason incompatible . See Observability.

title: SQLite
description: Run Runwick on one SQLite file for apps whose workers all live on one machine, with WAL and synchronous=FULL enforced.
body: The SQLite store keeps all of Runwick's data in one database file. It behaves like the PostgreSQL store: the same job states, retries, receipts, uniqueness and rate rules. It suits an app that runs on a single machine, in one process or several, and that does not want a database server. Requirements Item Requirement --- --- Engine SQLite 3.38 or newer. The bundled native library already is. Topology One file on a local disk. Every process that uses it runs on the same machine. Durability WAL journal mode and synchronous=FULL , on every connection Package Runwick.Sqlite (uses Microsoft.Data.Sqlite) Install and create the file Run the migration once before the app starts. It creates the file if needed, creates the tables and switches the file to WAL mode: Running it again does nothing if the schema is already current. Register the store The connection string must name a file with Data Source= . Runwick opens its own connections from it and never logs it. Option Default Allowed What it does --- --- --- --- WriterBusyTimeout 2 s 100 ms to 30 s How long a write waits for another process to release the file's write lock. ReaderThreads 2 1 to 8 Threads for read-only calls, each with its own connection. A value outside its range fails at startup with invalid policy . How the store uses threads The .NET SQLite library runs its "async" methods synchronously. So Runwick runs its database work on a few dedicated threads: one writer and ReaderThreads readers. The worker's lease and scheduling loops never wait inside a SQLite call.
