Durability: WAL and synchronous=FULL Every connection Runwick opens sets synchronous = FULL and foreign keys = ON , then reads the settings back. The file must be in WAL mode, which the migration sets once and SQLite remembers. A reply from the store means the commit is on disk, as far as your disk's fsync goes. If any of these settings does not stick, the store refuses to start with store profile mismatch . There is no "faster but less safe" mode. Setups that are refused Setup What happens --- --- In-memory database ( :memory: , Mode=Memory ), empty Data Source Refused at startup with invalid policy Mode=ReadOnly , Cache=Shared , Foreign Keys=False Refused at startup with invalid policy A file on a network share (a UNC path or network drive on Windows; NFS, SMB/CIFS, 9p, sshfs, Ceph, GlusterFS and similar on Linux) Refused at startup. The message names the filesystem type. A file not in WAL mode (for example, never migrated) Refused with store profile mismatch SQLite older than 3.38 Refused with engine version unsupported On Linux the check reads the mount table. A filesystem Runwick does not recognise as either local or network is accepted, but reported as unverified rather than verified. SQLite's locking only works between processes on the same machine. A file shared over the network can corrupt silently, which is why Runwick refuses it. A container volume is fine if every container that opens the file runs on the same host and the volume is a local disk. One writer at a time SQLite lets one transaction write to a file at once, across all processes. Every Runwick write takes that lock up front. Workers send routine work in batches (claim and start up to 32 jobs, renew up to 64 leases, finish up to 32 jobs in one transaction), so they wait for the lock and sync to disk once per batch rather than once per job. This has two practical effects: - Nothing here says SQLite matches PostgreSQL's throughput. Measure your own load. - While any write transaction is open on the file, every Runwick write waits, lease renewals included. A long transaction of your own on the same file can make leases expire. Keep them short. Polling There are no wake-up notifications between processes. Workers find new jobs by polling, which is enough for correctness. Within one process, a commit wakes that process's own workers, scheduler and outbox relay straight away. A job dispatched by another process is picked up on the next poll. Your transaction, the same file If your business tables live in the same SQLite file, you can create a job, or complete one, in your own transaction with ISqliteJobDispatcher and ISqliteJobCompletion . Your connection must use the same file and have foreign keys = 1 and synchronous = FULL . Begin the transaction with BeginTransaction(deferred: false) so it takes the write lock at the start: A SQLITE BUSY error from your transaction reaches you unchanged; retrying the whole transaction is up to you. See Transactions for the full rules. What SQLite does not promise - No multi-host support and no high availability. - No durability beyond your disk and its fsync behaviour. Restoring the file from a backup is a break in history. - A killed process is not a power-loss test. Runwick's tests claim crash consistency, not protection from a disk that lies about fsync. Next steps When SQLite fits, and when to move to PostgreSQL. Commit jobs with your own rows in the same file.

title: Delivery guarantees
description: What Runwick promises about running your jobs, how to make repeated runs harmless, and the list of things it does not claim.
body: Runwick is at-least-once. A confirmed job is not lost, but its handler can run more than once. Exactly-once is available in one case: effects inside the same database as the job store, through transactional completion. For everything else, use idempotency keys. At-least-once A handler can run again when: - the worker crashes after the work but before it records the result; - the worker loses its lease while the handler is still running (for example after a long pause), and another worker takes the job; - the reply from the store is lost, and the attempt cannot be settled in time. In each case Runwick runs the job again rather than risk losing it. So write handlers that are safe to repeat. When a dispatch is confirmed DispatchAsync returns a DispatchReceipt only after the store has confirmed the write. The receipt's ConfirmedAcknowledgementProfile says what "confirmed" means for that store: Store Confirmed means --- --- PostgreSQL the transaction committed SQLite the commit is on disk, with WAL and synchronous=FULL Redis the write is in the append-only file and synced, under appendfsync always If DispatchAsync throws an error whose Disposition is KnownNotApplied , nothing was written. If it throws DispatchOutcomeUnknownException (codes outcome unknown , cancelled after send or expired unknown ), the write may or may not have happened. Resolving an unknown outcome Do not simply dispatch again: that may create a second job. The exception carries the operation ID and the prepared request: A prepared dispatch keeps its operation ID, so sending it again replays the same command and never creates a second job. It is valid until its deadline (5 minutes by default). Dispatching covers IPreparedJobDispatcher in detail. Make repeats harmless: idempotency keys When a handler talks to something outside Runwick's database (an email service, a payment API, another database), pass a key that is the same on every run and let the other side ignore duplicates. A good key is stable and comes from the job, for example the job ID from IJobContext.JobId or a business ID in the payload. Many APIs accept an Idempotency-Key header for exactly this. The job ID stays the same across retries of one job. Do not use the attempt ID: it changes on every run. Uniqueness is not idempotency People say "idempotent" for three different problems. Runwick solves two of them. You want to avoid Use --- --- Two copies of a job queued at once UniqueWhileActive (an active key) A client retry creating a second job UniqueWithinWindow (a window key) Two jobs running at the same time for one resource A concurrency limit, for example PerResource(..., capacity: 1) A repeated run having a visible effect twice Idempotency keys in your handler, or transactional completion Dispatch uniqueness prevents a duplicate insert . It never promises that a handler runs once: retries and recovery can still run the one job more than once. See Uniqueness and Rate limits and concurrency. The one exactly-once case If the handler's effect is a change in the same PostgreSQL database or SQLite file as Runwick's tables, the change and the job's completion can commit together: Either both are saved or neither is. This covers effects inside that one database only. Redis has no transactional completion. Transactions has the rules. The outbox To create a job in a store other than your business database, the outbox commits a message with your data and a relay delivers it. Delivery is at-least-once, with de-duplication on the receiving side for a limited window (7 days by default). It is not exactly-once dispatch and it does not keep order. What Runwick does not claim - No exactly-once in general. A handler may run more than once. - Cancellation is cooperative. It cancels a CancellationToken . Your code must observe it. See Cancellation. - A lost lease does not prove the old handler stopped. Two copies can briefly overlap. Concurrency limits count valid leases, not code that is physically still running. Fencing tokens ( IJobContext.Fences ) help only if the resource you write to rejects lower values. - "Began" does not prove your code ran. A crash right after an attempt began is recorded as abandoned. - Timeouts measure the handler pipeline , not what happened in the outside world. There is no default timeout. - A restored database is a break in history. Receipts, uniqueness windows and fences from before the restore are not guaranteed to behave as one continuous record. - A schedule creates at most one job per occurrence , and that job is at-least-once like any other. Pausing a schedule does not pause jobs it already created. - Counts and metrics can be lost on a crash. They are not for billing or audit. - No high availability claim for any store. Failover and restored backups are outside what is tested. - No platform claims beyond what is tested : Linux x64 and Windows x64 on .NET 10. No claim for Native AOT or trimming.

title: Jobs and handlers
description: Define a job contract with a stable name, write the handler that runs it, and register both.
body: A job is a small data record that describes work to do. A handler is the class that does the work. Runwick stores the job, and a worker later decodes it and calls the handler. The job contract A job contract is a concrete class or record that implements IQueueJob . IQueueJob is an empty marker interface. Payloads are data only: they carry no behaviour, and attributes on them cannot resolve services or do I/O. Every contract needs a stable name . The name is what Runwick stores, so you can rename, move or re-namespace the class without breaking queued jobs. The CLR type name is never stored. You can use both. Identity settings ( [JobName] and Named , [PayloadVersion] and AtVersion ) must agree if both are present, or startup fails with identity conflict . For queue, priority and MaxExecutions the fluent value wins over the attribute. The full order is in Configuration. Attribute Fluent twin What it sets --- --- --- [JobName("x")] .Named("x") The stored name. Required. [PayloadVersion(n)] .AtVersion(n) The payload version. Default 1. [Queue("q")] .ToQueue("q") Default queue. Default default . [Priority("p")] .WithPriority("p") low , medium or high . Default medium . [MaxExecutions(n)] .WithMaxExecutions(n) Run budget, 1 to 100. Default 3. [UseJobMiddleware("alias")] .UseMiddleware("alias") Middleware by alias. Attributes are not inherited. A derived class never picks up its base class's name. Hangfire also has a QueueAttribute . If a file imports both, alias Runwick's: using JobQueue = Runwick.QueueAttribute; and write [JobQueue("emails")] . Naming rules Name Rule --- --- Job name 1 to 200 characters of A-Z a-z 0-9 . - , starting with a letter or digit Application, queue, pool, middleware alias Same characters, 1 to 128 Names are case-sensitive and never trimmed. A dotted style such as email.welcome or billing.invoice.send reads well in the dashboard. Two contracts with the same name fail startup with duplicate job name . The handler A handler implements IJobHandler with one method, HandleAsync(TJob job, CancellationToken cancellationToken) . - Returning normally means success. - Throwing an exception means a retryable failure, unless it is a PermanentJobFailureException . See Retries and timeouts. - The token is cancelled on a user cancel, a timeout, a lost lease or shutdown. Pass it to every awaited call. See Cancellation. Handlers are registered as scoped services. Runwick creates a fresh DI scope for every attempt, so a scoped DbContext belongs to that one attempt and is disposed afterwards. Inject anything you need into the constructor, including IJobContext (see Job context). Runwick is at-least-once. A crash after the work but before the result is saved runs the handler again. Make the effects safe to repeat. See Delivery guarantees. There is one handler per job name per worker. Binding two handlers to one job fails with duplicate handler . Registration Registration happens inside AddRunwick . Nothing is scanned automatically. Call What it does --- --- AddJobsFromAssemblyContaining () Registers every non-abstract class in that assembly that implements IQueueJob and has [JobName] . Classes without [JobName] are skipped. AddHandlersFromAssemblyContaining () Registers every class in that assembly that implements one or more IJobHandler , and registers each TJob . AddHandler () Binds one handler and registers its job. AddJob () Registers a contract and returns a builder to configure it. ConfigureJob () Configures a contract registered elsewhere. On its own it registers nothing ( job not registered ). Each scan only looks at the one assembly you point it at, and runs in a fixed order. Configuration is checked once, at startup. Runwick collects every error and throws one RunwickConfigurationException that lists them all, so a typo in a queue name stops the app before it does any work. Payload serialization Payloads are stored as UTF-8 JSON using Runwick's own fixed profile, runwick.json version 1. It does not use your ASP.NET JSON settings, so changing those can never change what is in the queue. The profile is strict: - Property names are camelCase. Unknown properties and duplicate properties are rejected when reading. - Numbers must be real JSON numbers. Enums are written as their member names. - DateTime values must be UTC. Prefer DateTimeOffset for instants. - Members typed object , [Flags] enums, [JsonConverter] and attributes that loosen the rules are rejected at startup. Use JsonElement for free-form data. - Polymorphism works only for closed hierarchies declared with [JsonPolymorphic] and [JsonDerivedType] . You can supply source-generated metadata with runwick.AddJsonTypeInfoResolver(MyJsonContext.Default) . Payload limits These limits are fixed. Dispatch fails before anything is written if a payload breaks them. Limit Value --- --- Serialized payload 1 MiB Nesting depth 32 levels One string value 256 KiB Properties per object 256 Elements per array 16,384 Keep payloads small. Store a file or a large document elsewhere and put its ID in the job. Changing a payload's shape The worker decodes the stored bytes fresh on every run. If you change the record, raise the version and register an upgrade from the old shape: Each step goes up by exactly one version. Upgrades run on the worker, after the run is authorized, and must be pure functions. A worker only picks up jobs whose version it can decode, so during a rolling deploy old workers leave version 2 jobs alone. More in Upgrades. Runwick.Contracts for shared job types Runwick.Contracts holds IQueueJob , the handler interface, the attributes and the dispatch types. It has no dependencies. Put your job records in a class library that references only Runwick.Contracts . Producers and workers both reference that library, and the library never pulls in database drivers or handler code. The app that actually dispatches still needs Runwick and a store package, because IJobDispatcher is implemented there. A producer-only app simply leaves out AddWorker and does not need the handlers.
